Building on our previous work regarding the maximum of symmetric two-variable functions, we examine the generalization error of a two-layer neural network with one hidden unit trained on a uniform distribution of points within a $d$-dimensional hypercube. Our findings indicate an increase in generalization performance as dimensionality increases, with the worst-case scenario occurring at $d \to \infty$. This approach offers two contributions: (1) determination of the optimal weights for the hidden layer under arbitrary input weights, which may not be uniformly distributed, to minimize worst-case generalization error, and (2) demonstration that training on the training set incurs no generalization penalty regardless of training set size.

Using data from the Pierre Auger Observatory covering 445 TeV of cosmic ray energy, researchers analyzed the 10-year all-sky distribution to investigate energy-dependent anisotropies. Results indicate that the dipole amplitude in the direction of the South increases from 1.3% at 4 EeV to 1.7% at 74 EeV, with statistical errors of 0.35 eV of the latter being 0.5-0.6% respectively, showing a clear energy escalation for sources above 4 EeV. Furthermore, the multipole composition shifts with energy, revealing a trend where higher energies at greater multiplicities dominate the distribution.

As an application, we examine the homogeneity of the limiting equation on these domains when the boundary roughness is of parabolic character.

Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) often forecast a favorable response to immunotherapies in various cancers, making their quantification a critical area for research. Although recent studies have quantified these cells using digitized tissue sections, current methods struggle with the high variability observed in staining and section preparation. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to estimate TIL density by segmenting nuclei within tumor regions. Nuclei were labeled in 199 breast cancer images, which were then classified into nine distinct color categories to reflect diverse visual appearances. The dataset was split into training (100 images), validation (20 images), and testing (the remaining 99 images). Nomenclature for TILs was established based on pathologist reports from 15 cases within the training/validation sets and applied consistently to all test images. Magneto-mechanical systems coupled with microwave cavities facilitate diverse forms of light-sound-matter interaction within the quantum regime. Leveraging the extensive phonon modes of two-dimensional materials, these arrangements promote sophisticated cavity magnomechanical quantum engineering. This article introduces a newly proposed configuration consisting of YIG films suspended over superconducting resonators supported by piezoelectric substrates. To enable precise control over both Stonewall-Einstein and Faraday effects, the configuration uses superconducting inductive/in-capacitance (LC) circuits coupled to multiple locations on the piezo-electric substrate. The LC circuits drive efficient interaction with the substrate's single dominant mechanical phonon mode, concentrating energy rather than scattering across numerous modes, thereby enhancing system coherence. To isolate and amplify coherent scattering within cavity magneto-mechanics systems, we suggest using pure LC circuits which offer minimal dissipation. Beyond improving coherence, this architecture supports advanced protocols such as coherent state preparation and measurement, quantum state teleporation, and quantum error correction within these multi-mode interactions.

This paper introduces a novel framework for quadrupedal robot adaptation to challenging locomotion scenarios, such as traversing steep inclines or complex outdoor environments. Our approach leverages a gated autoencoder and a reinforcement learning policy trained within a physics-based simulation environment utilizing a hybrid reward function. This combination facilitates the learned gait adaptations described above. Specifically, for intricate tasks like general exploration on uneven terrain or achieving maximum speed on stairs, the method proves its capability through two distinct avenues: first, by visualizing and analyzing the adaptive gaits themselves; second, by demonstrating superior performance metrics, specifically maximizing terminal torques on stairs and extending episode durations for arbitrary tasks compared to existing methods.

Hot winds are widely recognized as a critical component of galaxy evolution feedback; however, their generation within the sub-kiloparsec scales surrounding low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs) remains poorly understood. We conducted a multiwavelength analysis of M51, a nearby star-forming galaxy hosting an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH)-fed LLAGN, to address this gap. Our observations, which include Chandra X-ray data alongside new NIR and NIRJ sub-kilo-parsec resolution imaging from JWST, reveal a 12 kiloparsec-wide circumnuclear ring of star formation. We demonstrate that M51's inner and outer sub-kilo-parsec regions each host distinct, compact star-forming rings. Notably, the inner ring is significantly more compact than the galaxy's outer ring. We identify a previously uncharacterized Chandra source (C2) within M51's inner ring that exhibits hard X-ray emission and is likely an IMBH or similar LLAGN. We propose that the hot gas associated with this LLAGN may interact with the nearby star-forming inner ring, a scenario that could facilitate ring contraction.

This work addresses the acceleration of reinforcement learning within the transient phase when adapting an optimal regulator within the framework of continuous-time finite-horizon LQR. Employing a model-free approach, we propose an incremental learning algorithm that benefits from prior LQR runs by utilizing a series of finite-horizon tasks. We establish sufficient conditions to demonstrate that this series converges to an open-loop stable closed-loop system and provide a lower bound on inter-step horizon increments required for convergence. To enhance efficiency, we also introduce a multi-agent framework to accelerate the convergence rate during the transient response. The proposed methods are validated through numerical examples.

The SiD Detector features a comprehensive calorimeter system with an extended longitudinal depth, contributing to excellent jet energy resolution even at high energy levels. This segment outlines the techniques employed to optimize this resolution, including optimizing the jet definition, calibrating the detector response, enhancing signal collection through advanced algorithms, and reducing systematic uncertainties. Additionally, these methods effectively suppress background noise through targeted signal cuts and machine learning strategies.

Deep learning has emerged as a highly effective framework for addressing remote sensing challenges, particularly in spectral unmixing. While recent studies have introduced various deep learning models for this purpose, their real-world effectiveness remains difficult to assess. This limitation arises primarily from the absence of a standardized evaluation platform and the inconsistent reporting of methods and metrics across the literature. To address this, we introduce the EarthNets platform, a Web service designed to facilitate the comparison, benchmarking, and evaluation of deep learning approaches. Specifically, we present the first comprehensive evaluation platform centered on spectral unmixing, offering accessible metrics and an comparison of numerous methods within this domain. Additionally, we illustrate the platform's utility by analyzing the performance of these spectral unmixing techniques, an exercise that also provides insights into potential future advancements. The source code for the EarthNets platform is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/EarthSensingLab/EarthSensingLab.

This study investigates large-scale collective dynamics in two-dimensional active nematic fluids through extensive simulations, revealing that their behavior aligns with the paradigms of the conventional nematic phase observed in equilibrium systems. Specifically, we confirm the validity of the one-dimensional nematic scalar orientational order, the dynamic nematic scattering spectrum, and the orientational correlation's spatial decay. We also demonstrate active nematic hydrodynamic dynamics, where viscosity arises from nematic ordering; this hydrodynamic mode dominates if the fluctuation-dissipation relation holds. However, we identify the presence of unique characteristics in these active systems. First, the amplitude of orientational fluctuations is significantly elevated compared to standard equilibrium states. Second, the correlation between nematic ordering and velocity fields is altered. Leveraging this active matter-specific coupling between orientation and flow, we analyze hydrodynamic nematic ordering as a mechanism that drives long-range collective motion. This analysis provides crucial insights into the behavior of active nematic hydrodynamics, with implications for understanding biological membrane mechanics and optical nematic systems driven by laser light.

This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework, DRP-ResNet, designed to identify acute myocardial infarction within coronary angiography images. A core component of this method is a dynamic region partitioning scheme that segments coronary angiography images into non-overlapping areas, automatically delineating blood vessels and acutely infarct zones. This scheme outperforms grid-based segmentation methods in identifying abnormal regions, thanks to an integrated blood vessel segmentation module that incorporates vessel context. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate that DRP-ResNet surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods for detecting acute myocardial infarction.

This work examines how meson-loops involving two pions influence the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, $a_\mu$. Starting from the dispersion relation, we analyze the disconnected vacuum polarization diagrams and derive their impact on the hadronic light-by-light scattering contribution. Our findings indicate that the two-pion exchange through isospin-zero states drives most of the effect observed from correlated pion dynamics within energies up to $1\,\text{GeV}$. By employing the Regge model, we estimate the total contribution from two pion-muon diagrams at $40 \times 10^{-12}$, which aligns with recent estimates derived using the Regge model, by $40 \times 10^{-12}}$. Our estimate for the total muon anomalous dimension is $40 \times 10^{-12}}$, which is a significant result in the context of the Standard Model. This result highlights the importance of two-pion exchange in explaining the muon's magnetic moment. Our study provides valuable insights into the muon's behavior and supports recent models that utilize the Regge model to describe disconnected vacuum polarization diagrams. This research underscores the critical role that two pion-muon diagrams play within energy ranges below $40 \times 10^{-12}}$, which is a significant finding for understanding how muons behave under these conditions. Recent advancements in transfer learning for natural language have demonstrated remarkable success across diverse applications. Building on this momentum, researchers have recently explored pre-trained models within programming domains, yielding promising initial results. This survey offers a comprehensive overview of foundational elements in this emerging discipline. Following an examination of existing literature, we provide a systematic categorization of pre-trained models tailored to various processing levels of source code. Furthermore, we present an in-depth analysis demonstrating how these pre-trained models enhance downstream performance. To facilitate broader adoption, our investigation includes a repository of open-source pre-trained models alongside a thorough guide for leveraging them effectively.

This work details both the algorithm and its performance record for generating the 10-year (2008–2018) Mesoscale Atmospheric Radiation for the Clouds and the surface (METEOR) vertical aerosol optical depth (AOD) from wide-field photometry. The algorithm's main advantage is deriving AOD values without requiring a standard absolute calibration. During its first decade, the algorithm went through several major revisions, each bringing significant enhancements to both its scientific methodology and engineering reliability. The study concludes by presenting a 10-year global dataset and comparing the results against the Copernicus Global AOD dataset to demonstrate consistency.

Graphical Lasso provides a mechanism for recovering the conditional independence structure within graph-organized data. This study presents an adapted version of Graphical Lasso that supports non-convex penalties by introducing a two-step strategy. First, a partition of the parameter space is created by reparameterizing the problem through the inclusion of latent variables. Second, graphical models are estimated by alternately updating this latent information and solving non-convex optimization problems. This methodology generalizes the classic G-Lasso approach, making it applicable to a broader array of penalty functions while reusing well-established tools designed specifically for graphical models. By integrating extensive pseudo-observations into the analysis, we demonstrate that this latent variable framework yields superior initial value estimates, thereby enhancing the performance of state-of-the-art penalty selectors. Furthermore, empirical evaluations on both simulated and real-world datasets illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm.

We introduce a disk model designed to analyze the spectral signatures of circumstellar dust surrounding low-mass stars and brown dwarfs. In this framework, the total emission is separated into a free-free component, influenced by the star's X-ray output, and a thermal infrared component, driven by absorbed stellar radiation. We examine various disk structures, including configurations with smooth vertical density profiles and those featuring condensation fronts (snow lines). Our results demonstrate that the snow line generates a distinct inflection in the spectrum, pushing both disk components toward longer wavelengths. Additionally, we assess how observational limitations—specifically upper and lower bounds on detection—impact the inference of disk physical parameters. Our assessments of simulated observables are applicable to current facilities, such as the XMM-Newton X-ray telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope.

Traditional methods of extracting pitch values often fail when background noise is present, resulting in inaccurate detections. This paper introduces a self-driven, adaptive algorithm capable of rapidly and accurately identifying pitch even in noisy environments. Our approach begins by evaluating the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) to choose between two distinct auto-correlation algorithms: one optimized for clear signals and another tailored for noisy conditions. Furthermore, we implement a self-driven, narrowband, adaptive formant filter within the auto-correlation workflow. This filter dynamically adjusts based on the estimated fundamental frequency to enhance the corresponding auto-correlation peak. Experiments on speech recordings of varying quality demonstrate that the proposed algorithm surpasses existing approaches in both speed and accuracy.

We establish the convergence of this algorithm to a relevant alternative proof shows strong future directions for research and development in optimization methodology. It demonstrates significant robustness outperforming both strict acceleration and strict dual witness methods by avoiding instability issues inherent in these extreme cases. In practical terms, it acts as an advanced wrapper for the Anderson acceleration method that significantly improves its robustness.

Recent Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods employ deep learning-driven, black-box propabilities to evaluate candidate designs, disregarding the intrinsic properties of these programs. This study demonstrates that neural architectures identified through deep learning-based NAS exhibit consistent program characteristics. Specifically, we find that models with higher performance exhibit lower spatial complexity and more uniform computational pathways. These observations validate findings from prior non-neural research and suggest that such structural properties strongly correlate with modeling capability for vision tasks. Consequently, we introduce a resource-efficient, property-driven approach termed UFLP (Uniform Filtered Level-order Pruning) to enhance candidate architectures. Experimental results demonstrate that UFLP significantly boosts performance on the CIFAR-100 validation set across multiple keyword search benchmarks, achieving comparable accuracy while delivering 20–45% reductions in floating-point operations compared to unoptimized models.

This study presents an extensive evaluation of multicasting in millimeter-wave networks using realistic channel models and large-scale array configurations. The findings indicate that deploying multiple receiver antennas offers significant throughput and computational complexity reductions, with a simple greedy algorithm achieving nearly the same performance as more complex optimal approaches in large antenna systems. The paper further introduces and validates an efficient compressed sensing-based method for WSINR maximization with computational complexity scaling as $O(N^3)$; under this model, optimizing beamforming for over a thousand simultaneous users involving more than fifty thousand variables can be resolved in just a few seconds. The research confirms that mmWave multicasting achieves substantial performance gains, particularly when using multiple receiver antennas where small angular user clusters allow for even greater opportunities. Finally, comparing the considered compressed sensing approach against successive interference cancellation (SIC), simulations confirm that both achieve similar WSINR performance, although our method calculates nonorthogonal precoder power allocation coefficients rather than merely performing user detection and successive decoding.

This study introduces FDD, a communication-efficient approach for training neural networks on distributed datasets, which builds upon the concepts of Distillation and FedDistill while offering key improvements. Specifically, our proposed algorithm replaces traditional global model averaging with an ensemble distance optimization strategy to train local models. This design yields two primary advantages: it enhances resistance to backdoor attacks present in both FedDistill and FA, and it significantly reduces synchronization overhead by allowing updates to be aggregated asynchronously across multiple devices. Most notably, our inclusion of Quantization-Free Distillation as its core component allows the algorithm to drastically lower the quantity of data transferred between clients and the server without the computational penalties often associated with compression. Empirical results indicate that our method surpasses standard FedDistill in both efficacy and efficiency, particularly when dealing with large-scale models and diverse non-IID data distributions.

Service discovery and orchestration remain critical challenges in service-based systems (SBS), particularly within cloud environments where virtual services are delivered across distributed nodes. To address these issues, this study proposes Service Discovery Assisted Dynamic Orchestration (SDADO), an algorithm that enhances service delivery performance by minimizing end-to-end latency while maximizing system throughput through intelligent virtual service allocation. This minimization is achieved by directing users toward optimal orchestration paths based on both service intrinsic attributes and the dynamic states of providers. Furthermore, the SDADO protocol supports efficient load balancing by enabling services to migrate dynamically in response to fluctuating workloads and performance metrics. Empirical results derived from both MATLAB simulations and a cloud-based implementation indicate that the algorithm significantly lowers average latency and delays until more throughput compared to existing competing methods.

This study investigates the asymptotic stability of an inertial damped wave system defined on a metric graph with tree-like structure. The analysis centers specifically on cases where the central junction lacks elastic restoring forces on its connecting slopes. It is established that even without elasticity at this slope, exponential stability persists under specific matching conditions. Furthermore, an unstable mode is identified as a special instance in the broader class of dertained graphs. Finally, an explicit result regarding the determination of decay rates is provided.

This work investigates the nonperturbative structure and dynamics of color-flavor locking (CFL) in the presence of unequal matter densities ($U(1)_N$ symmetry breaking under inhomogeneous conditions). We find that the $\bar{q}q$ condensate emerges due to chiral symmetry breaking, driving the color triplet pairing in the quark sector ($\langle \psi_{L}\psi_{R}\rangle \neq 0$). This finding contradicts the standard nonperturbative calculations which predict no such condensate. We derive a set of coupled nonlinear equations to solve for the mass gap variables $\Delta$, $\mu$, and $\Omega$, finding that their solutions are sensitive to the unknown cutoff parameter; we suggest that these variables remain constant up to approximately $10\%$. We propose that these findings offer a new perspective on the instability of color-flavor locking inhomogeneous matter and suggest they may also influence quarkyonic matter stability.

MKTl4Te3 is a newly identified non-magnetic material that demonstrates exceptional transport characteristics, specifically high Hall conductivity, robust spin-orbit torque, significant spin accumulation, and superior spin diffusion ranges. These attributes render it an ideal candidate for next-generation spin-based technologies, including spin transistor systems and magnetic memory. The robust spin transport mechanisms in MKTl4Te3 stem from its tight spin-split valence bands, which are produced by strong spin-orbit coupling and favorable crystal symmetries. These properties have been experimentally verified through first-principles calculations. The comprehensive transport profile of MKTl4Te3 surpasses that of established heavy metals, such as W and Pt, and approaches the performance limits set by topological insulators, suggesting that this material can be integrated into practical, real-world devices.

An agent equipped with a utility function can optimize any task by maximizing expected utility; however, acquiring this function is challenging, particularly in offline reinforcement learning where access to a single trajectory is insufficient due to the inability to resolve all state values without further data. In knowledge-intensive domains like robotics and medicine, this function often encodes expert knowledge better represented as ordinal preferences over outcomes rather than quantifiable rewards. We propose training this function offline using Batch Optimization, a method derived from cooperative game theory that learns a utility function solely from the preferences over results provided by an optimizer. This approach is data-efficient compared to traditional methods using pairwise outcome data, avoiding the need for dense value functions over continuous states. We demonstrate the approach in two online reinforcement learning contexts by distilling policy knowledge: first, from a Black-Box Robot, and second, from a AlphaZero model.

This paper introduces a methodology for predicting future actions of agents trained via Reinforcement Learning using Sequence-to-Sequencemodels built from runtime observations. This capability offers valuable applications, such as predicting future decisions or detecting anomalies in this domain. Our evaluations show that this approach performs as effectively as methods requiring white-box access to the target agent and requires fewer resources than alternative data-driven solutions. Additionally, we explore and address a key challenge related to the unpredictability of random noise within the referenced agent system.

This study utilizes a matrix renormalization group method tailored for two-dimensional systems to examine the properties of the 3D herringbone lattice. We demonstrate that by introducing specific perturbations to the hopping term, one can transition the system from a metal to a band insulator. Furthermore, oncoming electrons experience an effective magnetic field when the potential energy parameter, $V$, is adjusted. By analyzing the system's density as a function of chemical potential within this generated effective magnetic field environment, we investigate and compare various ground states. Our findings reveal a remarkable analogy between the effects of the imposed effective magnetic field and those of a strong quantum Hall field, suggesting that tuning $V$ can sustain a state characterized by a fractional quantized Hall conductance.

In prior work, we addressed risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) within Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) by proposing parallel offline algorithms capable of generating near-optimal policies. That research assumed a fixed Mep, whereas the present study investigates the dynamic context where both Mep structures and reward functions may shift over time. We again propose parallel offline algorithms that establish performance lower bounds for risk-sensitive RL in this temporal context to a constant reference policy, demonstrating adaptability through the integration of restart mechanisms that have historically proven effective. Empirical simulations confirm that these offline algorithms remain highly effective in dynamic settings and that restart strategies are indeed crucial for achieving superior performance.

An extensive dataset comprising public Jira projects was compiled and made available for research into project configuration, usage patterns, and settings. Contributors can access the raw data in various formats, including JSON, XML, CSV, and XLSX, facilitating methods tailed to specific research questions. To support initial investigations, the authors also performed preliminary analyses and published corresponding findings in a dedicated companion document.

This paper investigates WPM (Weighted Power-Mean), a flexible family of aggregation functions capable of transitioning from sublinear to linear outcomes based on its parameter setting, and applies it to the distributed training of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Our analysis demonstrates that employing a sublinear WPM configuration enhances performance for both homogeneous and heterogeneous client scenarios in settings where data is non-IID across clients, outperforming standard all-round linear averaging. Conversely, allowing the WPM parameter to increase toward a linear setting helps mitigate communication bottlenecks during training while maintaining final DNN test accuracy. Experimental results confirm these observations, establishing WPM as an effective approach to improving both accuracy and communication efficiency in distributed machine learning.

We introduce an apparatus capable of emitting acoustic waves upon the de-excitation of a single atom trapped within a micro-cavity. This device functions by confining transitions that convert into phonons at the intersection point between an optical fiber and a levitated nanosphere. In this setup, the nanosphere serves a dual function: it acts both as the phonon-mode element of the micro-cavity and as the medium for optomechanical coupling. Initially, a trapped atom is excited using laser illumination; subsequently, as it cools down, energy is exclusively transferred into mechanical vibrations, resulting in the emission of sound. This configuration offers significant promise for developing on-demand, efficient acoustic sources with adjustable amplitudes and frequencies, thereby holding potential applications in quantum technologies, including precise depth profiling and transmutation depth imaging.

This work investigates valuated oriented graphs where each edge carries an integer weight, or “length.” We define a $k$-zigzag as an oriented path with exactly $k$ edges, and assign to it the minimum weight of all its closed extensions. Within this framework, we demonstrate that the space of $k$-zigzags equipped with this weight forms a metric space, and that its completion constitutes a $k$-neighborly oriented graph. Furthermore, we address a distance function defined by dividing graphs based on their connecting paths and present findings in this direction.

Although calculating the thermodynamics of a system of polymers is theoretically straightforward, the intricate interactions between long, tangled chains make direct computation nearly impossible. To address this challenge, we introduce a new approach where each polymer is defined by its constituent monomers arranged in a specific permutation. We term the dynamics of these monomers the "monomer soup," a framework that theoretically mirrors a viscous fluid but lacks corresponding physical evidence. Our analysis reveals two critical hurdles for this concept: first, a hidden length scale emerges within simulations, and second, monomer dynamics exhibit highly unusual characteristics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a newly proposed polymer-based free energy method is flawed because its theoretical foundation rests on an inconsistent ensemble.

Although a recent paper claimed to describe a system capable of supporting multiple patients with one ventilator while maintaining individual tidal volumes, this letter demonstrates through numerical simulations and theoretical analysis that, due to inherent nonlinearities in lung mechanics, maintaining a pre-set tidal volume is currently impossible under that proposed setup. Consequently, we conclude that this paper cannot yet ventilate patients using two circuits and a single ventilator while regulating each patient's tidal volume.

This article examines the groups of deck transformations arising from a simply connected covering of iterates on the Riemann sphere under a bicritical rational map, where exactly two critical points map to a single completely ramified point over the sphere. While previous work by others addressed the abelian case, our focus is primarily on demonstrating that these deck transformation groups are invariably finite for maps in this specific category, effectively resolving a question posed by Milnor and significantly advancing the understanding of their utility as tools for map classification.

This study examines a class of Bayesian single-index models incorporating a prior on the unknown regression coefficients and an improper prior for both the variance parameters and the nonparametric components. We demonstrate that accounting for an unknown error variance results in slower posterior contraction rates compared to a known variance scenario. Furthermore, we establish the rates of convergence for both parametric and nonparametric elements, showing that they achieve the optimal convergence rate applicable even in fixed-dimensional settings. Simulation analyses support our theoretical findings, confirming the validity of the proposed results.

Predicting component performance is vital for manufacturing, particularly when surface texture influences factors like friction, wear, and corrosion resistance. While image-based processing can quantify these textures using metrics such as Ra, Rq, and Rz, machining process parameters must be managed to achieve desired outcomes. This study examines the impact of various machining settings on texture by analyzing actual machined parts alongside their raw data. Results indicate that depth of cut exerts the most significant effect on surface roughness, followed by feed rate and spindle speed. While predicted values from image-based analysis align well with traditional calculations, these metrics demonstrate strong potential for assessing components that have reached the end of their service life.

We demonstrate that for a specific class of random graphs where edge weights are determined independently and at random, the infimum of all metrics equivalent to the natural combinatorial graph distance corresponds to an Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension context. In settings within this class that also feature stochastic equiconformality, the metric defining this Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension distance is identified as the graph random conductance distance. This result highlights connections to the theory of random fractals and the stochastic properties of graphs.

Deep learning techniques have proven highly effective in detecting signature forgeries, yet current research predominantly relies on synthetic samples consisting only of native and single-time forged signatures. This study introduces the Single-signature Multi-signature Forgery Detection Network (SMFDN), designed to enhance the generalizability of forged signature detection through a strategy of single-signature training and generalization. By leveraging the intrinsic features—distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability—of genuine signatures, the proposed model significantly improves overall performance. Extensive experiments were conducted to analyze how varying template characteristics and repeatability impact forgery recognition rates, yielding a state-of-the-art accuracy of 98.10% on a specific test set. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis was performed on three forgery categories, comparing the effects of varied template properties on the detection efficacy for different forgery types.

We perform an exhaustive analysis of supersymmetry constraints within D-brane effective actions, covering both ten-dimensional and four-dimensional string theories. This work identifies specific patterns linking instanton effects across various dual regimes to a universal mechanism consistently derived from supersymmetry constraints in string field theory. Furthermore, we determine the precise structure of the effective couplings in four-dimensional N=1 superconformal matter models by enhancing their global symmetries, yielding novel predictions for anomalies in both fermionic and bosonic matter components. Lastly, we resolve the specific anomalies in supersymmetric gauge theories by novel methods.

To investigate nitrogen evolution in the Milky Way, we utilized 3D galactic chemical evolution models to forecast nitrogen abundances across the galaxy's radial zones. These models accounted for both primary and secondary contributions to gas-phase nitrogen, comparing their outputs against observational data from various stellar populations, including the galactic center, outer regions, and halo. The model predictions for [N/O] ratios matched observational trends across the entire Milky Way, indicating that secondary nitrogen production plays a substantial role in the early Milky Way and remains significant today, although some primordial contribution persists. Furthermore, we examined how nitrogen evolves radially and temporally, finding that [N/O] ratios declined as oxygen abundance ([O/H]) decreased with galactic age and radius, suggesting sustained secondary production even in the current epoch. Additionally, we analyzed the correlation between [N/O] and metallicity ([Fe/H])), observing a trend similar in slope to the initial Milky Way sequence but with a reduced scatter, reflecting the higher relative importance of secondary production in the early galaxy. Finally, by applying a two-phase production framework, we determined the minimum levels of secondary yield for nitrogen relative to oxygen and estimated a minimum primordial nitrogen fraction ($y_{\rm N}^{\rm min}$) of approximately 0.05 at the 90th percentile of [N/O] distributions.

This research explores multilingual Natural Language Processing (NLP) studies, focusing on low-resource languages and presenting findings from a survey conducted by students and mentors during the 2021 NTU Multilingual NLP Workshop. These outcomes synthesize key aspects of a specialized subfield, demonstrating how recent advances in AI can benefit diverse global communities, including specific projects involving Malayalam and Maori. The workshop also showcased 21 proposed future research tracks and applied problems, emphasizing the centrality of multilingual NLP in the era of large-scale pre-trained models.

Network analysis of networked data and graph topology has become essential for understanding complex biological phenomena armed with extensive, high-dimensional molecular profiles. This paper introduces a new spatially-aware Signed Boolean Network (SABN) framework that integrates multi-modal data types—including copy number variations, expression levels, and mutations—while preserving crucial graph structural insights significant for identifying functional cell states. We further present a Markov Switch process-based approach to classify cells by leveraging the graph's fundamental topological characteristics. Validated across three major cancer cohorts and one normal tissue dataset, our methodology effectively maps normal tissue architecture and reveals distinct spatial tissue zones within breast, colon, and lung cancers. Notably, in mutation-rich regions, our model uncovers novel, mutually exclusive pathways governing the transition from health to disease.

The paper investigates a self-conjugate bi-doublet extension within the Left-Right Symmetric Model (SRSB) in light of recent observations of white dwarfs. We derive specific astrophysical constraints on the model's parameter space, particularly distinguishing between a CP-even and a CP-oceven mixtures. Our findings indicate that, from a purely white dwarf-based astrophysical standpoint, nearly the entire allowed parameter space remains viable. However, we also address cosmological implications, specifically constraining the model's ability to function as a dark matter candidate.

Recent studies indicate that employing edge-computing devices enhances image privacy classification accuracy by leveraging graph-structured data and neighboring information. Although existing models focus on graph properties relevant to images, they fail to address the intricate relationships within graph nodes and edges. The proposed Graph Privacy Advisor (GPA) improves these traditional models by utilizing an enhanced, learned representation through the attention mechanism. GPA's accuracy was tested on the recently introduced Privacy Benchmark (P2P) dataset, where it achieved the highest accuracy at 92.2%. Furthermore, GPA's capacity to detect the specific features in the P2P dataset most relevant to privacy classifications was validated.

This study investigates how quantum-statistical entanglement influences the entropy flow within radiation fields emitted by systems thermalized via the canonical ensemble. Specifically, we contrast two frameworks: the standard canonical ensemble and the Rindler quantum state characterized by Unruh radiation. Within the Rindler model entropy flux originates from zero-point fluctuations inherent to quantum mechanics and thermal fluctuations from classical statistics; however, entanglement modifies thermal fluctuations such that they thermalize system energy levels. In both cases—the standard ensemble and the Rindler state—the entanglement correction manifests as the Bose-Einstein distribution. When examining the entropy flux itself, we find that according to the first law of thermodynamics, the contribution of entanglement obeys conservation. In the Rindler context, the entanglement term adds a correction that strictly adheres to the first law. Furthermore, we analyze the interaction between entanglement and the interplay between quantum systems and their environment, exploring how these factors jointly determine the entropy flux in both models.

The ALICE detector at the LHC investigates jet modifications within central Pb+Pb collisions tagged by a photon on event side. Event sides containing high-$p_{\rm T}$ tagged jets are analyzed, with results presented as functions of the tagged jet's transverse momentum for both inclusive and photon-tagged jets in terms of their longitudinal momentum balance. Comparisons reveal distinct differences in the modification patterns between inclusive and associated jet scenarios, especially for photons of high pT, indicating parton shower contributions play a role. For central heavy ion collisions, the observed modifications align with previous ALICE findings showing no significant dependence on $p_{\rm T}$ up to approximately 20 GeV/$c$.

Recent advancements in computational methods for model comparison and selection leverage large-scale numerical simulations to generate datasets capable of training machine learning models capable of learning complex patterns not always evident in traditional data sources. These techniques allow for reduced simulation costs while improving model inference accuracy, benefiting from emerging low-precision hardware architectures anticipated to further reduce future computation times and storage requirements. This paper provides an overview of these novel approaches along with a demonstration applying them to invert three-dimensional magnetospheric models using a neural network based on observed particle data from space missions.

The FOXSI small satellite instrument suite is designed to conduct pioneering observations of the quiet Sun across the 0.5 to 2 keV energy band. A primary hurdle in detecting hard X-ray radiation from a quiet solar region is the overwhelming instrumental background noise; however, this signal can be significantly mitigated through active cooling and cooling systems that reduce background levels to levels where solar signals become discernible. By recording images with a superior spatial resolution of 0.6 arcseconds, these small satellites enable researchers to examine fine spatial structures and refine models regarding the energetic particle dynamics responsible for quiet solar emissions. This introductory report provides an overview of the scientific background, describes the instrument setup and performance metrics, reviews recent data results, and outlines upcoming scientific endeavors involving this instrument network.

Optimizing functions of non-commuting operators constitutes a fundamental challenge in quantum field theory and quantum information. This study investigates the task of determining optimal paths within a group of Euler-Arnold equations defined on a Lie algebra. Specifically, the research examines Eul-er-Arnold equations associated with a bilinear form on the Heisenberg group to construct solutions through the exponential map applied to a specific subspace spanning an optimal trajectory. Elopation via the exponential function yields group elements constituting optimal paths on the Heisenberg group. The results demonstrate that applying these methods enables the precise calculation of optimal paths characterized by the minimization of a cost quadratic function of a specific operator sequence. These findings also clarify optimal paths associated with quantum gates in quantum computing and show their relation to quantum circuits. As an illustrative example, the paper derives optimal paths on the SU(2) group by applying Eulers equations derived on su(2), demonstrating how these optimal solutions relate directly to optimal circuits in quantum computing and quantum gates therein. These results establish a foundation for further investigations into broader applications within the fields mentioned.

This work addresses sensor fusion in pose estimation by incorporating more generic correlations into our modeling of measurement errors. We propose that instead of relying solely on unidirectional correlations, the measurement errors should be modeled using bidirectional correlations to enhance representation. Within our measurement model, we utilize a stochastic relationship to describe the correlation between measurements, thereby improving the overall precision of our sensor fusion algorithms. Furthermore, our approach is more flexible by relying less on specific knowledge of the correlation structure, which proves particularly advantageous in practical applications where such details are often difficult to ascertain. We have implemented these principles in a modified Kalman filter, along with a corresponding innovation covariance calculation method. Finally, we validate our methodology through experiments involving realistic data from a mobile robot performing tasks in various indoor environments.

This study explores how cosmological multipliers from higher-dimensional branes could resolve the tensions between laboratory measurements of the dark matter-nucleon cross section across various energy scales. The proposed framework utilizes a "multi-temperature universe" concept, enabling a scale-dependent analysis of both the relic density and different observational probes. We propose a specific brane scenario capable of reproducing the standard cosmological evolution while offering an alternative dark matter solution, ultimately determining the brane positions and their effects on different scales to assess compatibility with experimental data.

We propose a new colorization framework that converts black-and-white images into colorful ones using domain adaptation and style transfer techniques. A key distinction of our method is its ability to decouple domain adaptation from colorization, enabling application across various domains beyond just grayscale restoration. Additionally, to enhance both efficiency and output quality, we introduce a shared network architecture that simultaneously handles multiple input domains, reducing computational demand while maintaining effectiveness. During the specific phase of converting shared representations into final colors, we incorporate a coding-based approach inspired by style transfer to enrich color variety and vibrancy. Experiments demonstrate that the method is highly efficient, delivering superior qualitative outcomes, and proves flexible enough to handle multiple grayscale domains effectively.

Shared coding environments, such as Google Docs for code, facilitate seamless real-time collaboration among programmers. Our examination of thirty-two public Google Docs repositories aimed to understand shared document creation and maintenance practices. We observed that while some repositories meticulously preserve peer contributions, others neglect upscaling, often overwriting others' work. Our findings also reveal distinct author hierarchies in these environments; despite equal contribution levels, few coders recognize the dominance of few individuals. Ultimately, this study offers valuable insights for scholars and practitioners seeking to enhance collaborative encoding and document sharing strategies.

We conducted a comprehensive astrometric and photometric review of the bipolar jet-associated binary system, BD And, utilizing observational data collected between 2017 and 2023 alongside literature reports for over four decades. Our photometric analysis indicates the presence of prominent ellipsoidal variations and distinct ellipsoidal polarization effects within the BD And binary pair; notably, observations collected so far preclude evidence for a third body in this system. Astrometric investigations identified a significant perturbation in the binary's orbit that commenced around 2017 and continues to the present. This deviation aligns with hypothesized influences exerted since approximately 2015, a period marking a jet eruption event. While this orbital perturbation and its timing coincide well with the 2015-2017 jet eruption event, we conclude that current data do not support a model where the perturbation was caused by a third stellar body. Instead, these findings indicate that both the binary eclipse timing variations and the associated jet eruption likely stem from internal dynamical interactions within jet-driven accretion processes.

We analyze the weighted least squares algorithm for Regressions with exact observations, assuming access to $N$ exact data points per frequency. This method guarantees error-free reconstruction when $N=1$, and approaches optimal performance as $N \to \infty$, while maintaining stability beyond the Nyquist-Shannon theorem for $N > 1$. Our weighted least squares approach handles cases that previous algorithms did, while also having the advantage of being computationally efficient. Specifically, our weighted least squares algorithm yields an upper bound on reconstruction error equal to the sum of squared distances between the observed function values and their corresponding theoretical estimates. As an illustration, we use this technique to derive new upper bounds on the total variation distance between a uniform distribution on $[0,1]$ and its discrete approximation using $N$ samples.

The analysis of light hadronic interactions with X(3872) was performed using the 2018 EPOS-LHC model, while interactions involving X(3872) were calculated by adapting this EPOS framework to account for the unique mass and internal makeup of the X(3872) particle. These modified or specialized interaction models were integrated into a 3+1 dimensional relativistic viscous hydrodynamic simulation to explore their effects on thermal equililibration and the rates of X(3872) production. The local moment interactions characteristic of disordered semiconductors like Si:P typically emerge from Coulomb forces between hole spins and the Coulomb or exchange forces acting upon unpaired electron spins. This study simulates such a system using the Ising model, where spins are restricted to a finite set of sites, each holding a specific degeneracy. By calculating the single-particle density of states (DOS) via a spectral Green's function method and the total DOS via a canonical finite-size method, we find excellent agreement for the impurity band DOS with Coulomb-interaction variational theory. Specifically, our simulation results for Coulomb interactions align with Green's function single-particle DOS theories for impurity bands derived by MacKinnon and Alexander. These findings allow us to extend the impurity band DOS theory to systems involving hole-spin/electron-spin interactions, suggesting that spin-spin interactions of this nature dominate the impurity band DOS in Si:P. Consequently, we propose utilizing these "local moment" models to investigate critical phenomena in Si:P and analogous disordered semiconductors.

This work investigates both perturbative and non-perturbative aspects of scalar field theories characterized by global U(1) symmetry, incorporating explicit symmetry breaking via cubic interactions. We determine renormalization constants using diagrammatic techniques to enable calculations in volume V, even as V approaches infinity. We demonstrate that, despite explicit symmetry breaking in specific diagrams, the conservation of the associated U(1) current holds non-perturbatively up to O(V⁻¹⁰). Furthermore, we analyze how this breaking influences mass degeneracy in two- and three-point correlation functions both within and beyond perturbation theory, finding that non-perturbative effects yield correlation functions consistent with perturbative predictions. Additionally, we assess the impact of vacuum instability on renormalization constants and calculate the transition rate for one- particle decay using a resummation of diagrammatic contributions. We find that this decay probability is directly proportional to the symmetry breaking parameter. Finally, we compute non-perturbative expressions for the transition rate, showing excellent agreement with perturbative estimates.

This paper introduces a framework designed to facilitate robot acquisition of expert demonstrations within real-world settings plagued by unknown confounding factors. By employing a hierarchical Bayesian model, we transfer learned estimates of these confounders from a population of peers equipped with prior robot Bayesian learning to individual target robots. This process enables the robot to bypass unknown interference elements while replicating human-like movements. We demonstrate the application of this method in a complex task involving the manipulation of a viscous liquid, showing that confounders estimated from a small subset of demonstrations are sufficient to guide the robot toward achieving the task successfully.

Let $G$ denote a locally compact quantum group, with its full discrete dual identified as the locally compact topological space $\widetX_H$. This paper investigates various topologies applicable to $\widetX_H$, specifically examining scenarios under which the whisker topology aligns with either the lasso or the stick topology. It further derives sufficient conditions to guarantee that the whisker, lasso, and stick topologies are coherent on $\widetX_H$, notably when $G$ possesses properties of compactness or is dual to a reduced group.

Motion planning is traditionally an independent stage that feeds into the reinforcement learning training process. This study introduces a novel deep reinforcement learning method where motion planning concepts are integrated directly into reward functions and policy structures. By doing so, motion training for autonomous vehicles is treated as a sequential decision-making process. Empirical evaluations show this approach surpasses existing methods regarding sample efficiency and robustness. Additionally, we propose a new reward concept that mitigates oscillatory behavior often observed in deep reinforcement learning training.

Although the formation of black holes (BHs) in early galaxies is linked to early massive stars, the mechanisms behind their rapid growth remain unclear. This study investigates the minimum possible mass of a central supermassive BH, independent of star formation rates. By modeling gas accretion driven by the Eddington-type disk surrounding a central BH—a scenario representing the most efficient possible growth—we determine the equivalent mass accreted by the cluster over typical star-formation timescales. This "true" accreted mass exceeds the stellar mass formed because much of the consumed gas bypasses stellar formation and falls directly to the central BH. Applying this "unstellarized" mass to observations of high-redshift galaxies, we find that even under optimal, unstaralized conditions, existing constraints on central BHs are still exceeded by at least a factor of 10. These results indicate that rapid, efficient gas accretion is sufficient to explain Supermassive Black Hole growth in early宇宙 structures when the contribution of direct accretion from the cluster to the observed masses is fully considered.

A significant advancement in recent years within machine learning has been the widespread adoption of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for image recognition tasks. Despite their superior accuracy, deploying these models in safety-critical scenarios necessitates not just confidence in predictions, but also a measure of uncertainty to ensure reliable decision-making. This study examines two distinct approaches for quantifying uncertainty in deep learning-based classification: temperature scaling and Monte Carlo dropout. Findings indicate that both methods effectively enhance uncertainty estimation during inference, correlating strongly with improved classification accuracy and the precise identification of out-of-distribution samples. Nevertheless, when evaluated across diverse datasets, there is no universal superiority among these techniques.

This study utilizes an extensive dataset of life science publications to evaluate whether authors should submit preprints prior to formal journal submission. By examining data gathered between 2013 and 2017 from four major institutions—Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, the Max Planck Society, the Flatiron Institute, and the Whitehead Institute—we assessed whether releasing findings early accelerates publication timelines and increases citation counts, all while addressing potential concerns regarding the validity of uncited peer-reviewed work.

Our findings indicate a clear trade-off: while sharing preprints may delay standard publication relative to the timeline of a typical research lifecycle, they significantly boost both total citations and per-article citation rates, a phenomenon observed regardless of the publishing venue. These results hold true even for articles undergoing rigorous peer review, effectively mitigaling concerns regarding quality.

Furthermore, this research underscores the critical need for granular, granular-level publication metadata to substantiate data-driven decisions in academic workflows. By demonstrating that preprint sharing enhances scholarly impact without compromising research integrity, the study advocates for wider adoption of such practices within the scientific community.

This paper introduces an integrated, automated system designed for the electronic documentation of laboratory tests and analyses, named ELAB (Electronic Laboratory). A primary objective in developing this system was to minimize human intervention to prevent errors associated with manual data handling. By utilizing a standardized approach to information capture, the architecture ensures compatibility with varying laboratory environments. Specifically, we designed and implemented an information model grounded in domain-specific knowledge to facilitate robust data representation tailored to diverse laboratory activities, demonstrating how such shared contextual understanding guides effective electronic health record architecture. To validate this electronic laboratory framework, we conducted a study interpreting the results of the COVID-19 pandemic testing rollout across two Canadian institutions, utilizing the COVID-19 data collected during this period. Furthermore, we evaluated the application of this laboratory framework within the context of developing a comprehensive, interoperable, and generalized electronic medical record architecture.

Recent years have seen significant advancements in applying machine learning to predict and analyze complex materials systems, including predicting phase formations, mechanical and thermal properties, discovering new alloys, and refining existing materials. These recent developments have been propelled by open-source databases, extensive experimental records, and the growing adoption of collaborative, decentralized initiatives. Nevertheless, significant hurdles remain regarding data availability for diverse systems, the pervasive uncertainty inherent in materials design, and the challenges associated with integrating legacy knowledge. This review examines current progress and identifies critical obstacles in employing machine learning for materials science, highlighting strategies to mitigate these issues through methods such as active learning, Bayesian modeling, transfer learning, data augmentation, and data compression. Finally, we explore emerging educational programs designed to equip the next generation of scientists with necessary computational literacy and collaborative research skills.

We compute the partial widths of the $T_{cc}^{+}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ system into its low-lying open-charm baryon-pair final states. The process begins by analyzing the strong interactions between the $T_{cc}^{+}$ molecule and these baryon pairs using the effective field theory of hadronic molecules. Within this framework, the contributions from intermediate $D\bar{D}$ and $\bar{D}$ states are evaluated at the loop level with on-shell conditions to derive the corresponding short-range form factors for the transition into $\mu^{-}\mu^{-}$. Finally, the partial widths are obtained by applying these short-range form factors within the standard electroweak point-interaction model for virtual lepton pairs. Our analysis reveals that, for the $ \mu^{-}\mu^{-} $ decay channel considered, the strong interaction effects stemming from $D\bar{D}$ baryon final states significantly exceed those from $D\bar{D}$ baryon final states. Consequently, the virtual $D\bar{D}$ baryon final states can be neglected in this specific context, thereby facilitating the interpretation of the measured branching fractions for the $ \mu^{-}\mu^{-} $ mode to extract properties regarding the $T_{cc}^{+}$ bound-state structure.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a significant area of research within machine learning, characterized by learning with graph-structured data. Subspace learning represents a fundamental challenge in machine learning, often addressed by representing data as graph structures, thereby mapping data points to the graph's vertices. In this context, graph embedding aims to identify data points embedded directly within the graph, potentially revealing intrinsic data patterns more effectively. This paper introduces a novel subspace learning approach utilizing graph neural networks alongside the concept of graph commutativity to identify and separate data points based on multiple latent subspaces. The proposed method was validated through experiments on various synthetic and real-world datasets, which confirmed its superior performance relative to existing techniques.

Recent work by non of the authors establishes that two complete Sidon sets within the finite affine plane, $\mathrm{AG}(\mathbb{2},q)$, correspond precisely to the elliptic projective spectrum of $P(\mathbb{2},q)$. In this paper, we provide an explicit construction based upon those elliptic curves while also addressing the analogous completeness problem for $\mathrm{AG}(\mathbb{2},q)$ over prime powers $q$ where $2$ is a quadratic residue. Our solution yields a new family of complete Sidon sets by leveraging the properties of parabolas and hyperbolas. Additionally, we outline the structure of elliptic curves over such fields to fully resolve these geometric configurations for all finite fields $\mathrm{AG}(\mathbb{2},q)$.

This study investigates the $k$-Set Cover problem on binary matrices, proposing the Non-uniform Sampling algorithm. Given a matrix with $n$ rows, this method selects one of $m$ specified subsets of these rows as a column based on probabilities defined by a probability distribution. Our results demonstrate that employing this non-uniform distribution over uniform sampling saves a factor of $\Omega(\sqrt{m})$ in the worst-case scenario while maintaining an approximate solution, where $\epsilon$ denotes the permissible approximation gap. Specifically, if a solution within a factor of at most $\epsilon$ obtained via uniform sampling exists (where $\epsilon > 0$ is not extremely small), our algorithm successfully finds an $\epsilon'$ solution with $\epsilon' = \epsilon + \delta$ using $O(\delta^2)$ fewer samples on average. Additionally we show that our results are optimal up to constant terms. Finally we also present some experiments and results showing how this algorithm performs better than state-of-the-art algorithms in practice.

XFitter is a Bayesian program designed for fitting parton distribution function (PDFs), enabling constraints to be derived from experimental data while quantifying associated uncertainties. This quantification is vital for determining the probability associated with various PDF applications, especially given recent shifts toward lower evolution scales in fitting procedures compared to traditional ones. Lower scales prevent direct comparison with data by leaving higher-order distribution information unfitted, a scenario addressed by XFitter through simultaneous fits at both a low input scale and a higher comparison scale via DGLAP evolution, ensuring compatible data alignment. Additionally, XFitter incorporates Lattice QCD results through Bayesian constraints without restricting usage to quark sea distributions alone.

Designed to enhance performance and scalability through a modular architecture, this system supports parallel execution of tasks on multi-core processors to accommodate larger datasets more efficiently. By employing this approach to distribute work, we can significantly enhance performance and achieve more efficient use of computing resources when handling large datasets that would otherwise require excessive time to process. Using various data mining tasks as a use case demonstrates how this package improves both the efficiency and effectiveness of data analysis workflows involving complex, resource-intensive operations necessary to derive meaningful insights from large volumes of data that would otherwise result in suboptimal use of computational resources when using standard single-core

This work examines the long-term dynamics of quasi neural networks operating in a finite layer configuration but with infinite width. The behavior of these networks is modeled as a system of nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) governed by the parameters of the architecture. We demonstrate that the decay rate of the neural tangent kernel's dominant eigenvalue—specifically its dependence on width—determines the network's asymptotic action, which can be reduced to linear ODEs. Furthermore, by addressing a key concavity issue regarding the quasi NKE's Jacobian, we show that this kernel remains close to the original NKT, even in the non-ideal network setup, thereby establishing proximity between their solutions. These findings extend existing results on standard neural networks to include cases with fully connected architectures without bias terms.

We examine the axioms defining a class of solutions to the solvable lattice model equation and demonstrate that for a pair of such models, local state probabilities correspond to the branching rule. These specifics include their explicit formulation through a rule-based approach, their connection to the T-system, and their relation to quantum group sl_2; in this context, the local probabilities are expressed in terms of the Wess-Zumino invariant, the Clebsch-Gordan invariant, and the quantum integer.

This work examines merging distinct stabilization methods within the framework of convex cone intersection problems, specifically targeting robustness issues in compressed cone detection. By integrating two existing algorithms, we create a hybrid approach that leverages interior point methods combined with projected gradient descent, allowing to simultaneously maintain algorithmic strengths. Crucally, we introduce a theoretical framework that analyzes how this hybridization affects signal recovery performance. Our analysis reveals that certain problems yield superior outcomes using this hybrid algorithm compared to applying individual stabilization methods. Furthermore, we conduct extensive numerical evaluations across various scenarios, demonstrating that the proposed algorithms are effective and yield comparable signal recovery performance with significantly reduced computational runtime.

Coadding images serves as a basic yet vital procedure in modern astronomy, which has been supported by numerous software tools ranging from simple Unix scripts to complex frameworks like DRizzleAlign in DRizzle. While most standard algorithms are designed for linear combination and preserve consistent Point Spread Function (PSF) profiles—whether for point sources or galaxies—this preservative quality is not shared by nonlinear methods such as clipped-mean or the median. To address this inconsistency, we introduce a diagnostic tool that evaluates coaddition performance and compares it to a reference single exposure with a matching PSF profile. The comparison focuses on two metrics: the Point Spread Function (PSF), representing the image of a point source, and the Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM), particularly relevant for extended objects. Our analysis employs simulated inputs and real data from the COSMOS field processed via DrizzleAlign to test the methodology. While Drizzle was run with various clip thresholds and processing times to gather a robust dataset for evaluation, results indicate that nonlinear combinations produce a PSF that deviates significantly from that of a single exposure, dependent on clip thresholds and duration. We also compare these findings with DSSO (our implementation of clipped-mean) and DrizzleAlign using Drizzle combinations across diverse clip thresholds and processing times to gather a robust dataset for evaluation.
