This study introduces a new statistical model, designated as MS(2)-AR(4)), tailored for electricity demand analysis. We utilize time series data from an Australian residential consumer to calculate this model, leveraging the multi-state nature characteristic of residential electricity usage. Primary focus is placed on modeling the autocorrelation structure inherent in the time series through a hybrid approach combining multi-state and autoregressive mechanisms. Furthermore, this proposed framework allows for more intuitive parameter estimation compared to traditional methods. Our analysis reveals that the MS(2)-AR(4)) model outperforms standard autoregressive models in capturing the electricity demand dynamics associated with the time series under examination.

It is crucial for public sector practitioners to recognize potential biases in web search outcomes so they may mitigate these distortions within their work. To investigate possible gender biases in search results for various professions, we conducted an empirical study utilizing log data from the open-source search engine, Weevely. By examining the autocomplete suggestions for roles such as programmer, nurse, and lawyer, we employed an algorithmic sentiment analysis to assess the gendered tone implicit within user suggestions. Our findings revealed significant gender biases in both the language users employ and the assistance search engines provide. To assist professionals in counteracting these biases, we recommend implementing strategies such as employing diverse keyword sets, cross-referencing different search platforms, and consciously refraining from automatic assumptions drawn from search suggestions.

This paper introduces a program synthesis framework capable of producing a single execution path for symbolic relationships across diverse input-output datasets. By performing a breadth-first search guided by heuristics for the program's structure and architecture, the method successfully identifies a logical solution within acceptable time limits in 92% of cases. On average, it synthesizes a program 100x faster than previous approaches, achieving improvements ranging from 10 to over a million times faster than baseline frameworks. When executed against golden datasets—comprising programs written by expert developers—the proposed method replicated 87.5% of their logical paths. This indicates that, unlike most prior program synthesis methods that yield only one specific solution, this approach can generate multiple valid programs from identical input-output examples.

Comprehensive models of Earth's climate rely on numerous coupled physical mechanisms. Due to their complexity, these climate systems require mathematical reduction techniques that yield simplified representations suitable for large-scale ensemble forecasting, climate sensitivity analysis, and the identification of long-term statistical behaviors. This presentation provides an overview of current reduction approaches, with specific emphasis on projection-based methods derived from observational data and the isolation of invariant manifolds. We offer numerical examples applying these strategies to the climate model ECHAM6 within the context of natural variability and responses to natural forcing agents.

A massive neutron star collision event, known as a kilonova, generates r-process material through the formation of a rapidly rotating remnant or directly ejected matter. This phenomenon produces emission lines arising from electron transitions in highly ionized atoms within a dense, dense environment of ejection. Observing these fine-structure lines in the infrared (IR) is crucial for understanding kilonova physics, a task best suited for the upcoming Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) due to its superior capabilities. This study investigates the feasibility of detecting the 2.15 $\mu$m [Ni II] fine-structure line from a kilonova using the ELT. We estimate the signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio achievable by applying an optimized, simple point spread function subtraction technique during ELT's 300-second exposure. For a source at a distance of 100 Mpc, this observation yields an S/N of 100. This performance indicates that the ELT will be uniquely capable of detecting and precisely measuring the 2.15 $\mu$m [Ni II] line in future events, whereas this line would remain undetectable by any existing facility. Furthermore, this line serves as a potential future marker for identifying other major cosmic events, such as core-collapse supernovae and black hole formation.

Although radiation oncologists face significant challenges obstructing the path of X-ray beams, existing evidence suggests that directional changes do not necessarily compromise the precision of targeting cancer cells. To better address these hurdles, researchers propose employing directional X-rays generated via gamma-ray interactions with magnetic fields within a cyclotron. By potentially eliminating the need for traditional accelerators, this magnetic field method offers a promising pathway to enhance treatment accessibility and effectiveness.

Compositional data consists of high-dimensional vectors constrained to the non-negative orthant of $\mathbb{R}^{d-1}$, with sum-to-one restriction on their components. A prevalent technique for analyzing such data involves applying the logarithmic ratio transformation to the vector parts to eliminate scale dependency. Post-transformation, the resulting variables reside on a specific manifold within $\mathbb{R}^{d-1}$ known as the log-compositional data format. This transformation yields variables that cannot be directly utilized in standard linear models or regression frameworks. This paper introduces a technique for linearly predicting transformed compositions using an orthogonal series within an $L^2$ space. We evaluate the method's performance on simulated data sets as well as real-world examples, comparing the results against established methodologies.

We introduce a statistical framework that examines how gas in a protoplanetary disk dissipates and impacts the formation of gas giants, utilizing this model to contrast simulated exoplanet systems—built to reflect diverse disk scenarios—with actual exoplanet and stellar data. This method highlights a significant mismatch: while the common view that planets form via core accretion typically involves an inevitable phase of runaway gas accretion, current observations of exoplanets fail to show signs of this runaway phase. This discrepancy suggests either that core accretion does not always trigger runaway gas accretion under various conditions or that disk evolution differs from prior assumptions. To test these alternatives, we compare predictions against a broader dataset including stellar ages, masses, disk lifetimes, and compositions. These comparisons favor a view where Jupiter analogues formed through significant gas accretion but were subsequently stripped of their atmospheres due to shorter-than-average disk lifetimes, implying that the existence of hot Jupiters offers evidence for modified disk evolution rather than exceptions to core accretion itself.

A key capability for intelligent systems is maintaining a memory trace of past events. In this work, we introduce a dynamic memory architecture enabling reinforcement learners to infer unobserved system states and refine predictions based on incomplete observations. By updating a memory tensor with latent features of sequential partial observations, an agent learns a robust representation of its history, which serves as a foundation for state tracking. Guided by this memory, agents can forecast future inputs and outputs while maintaining predictive stability despite variations in starting conditions or memory content. This enhanced forecasting skill, driven by memory, allows agents to acquire complex tasks that remain out of reach for models lacking such mechanisms.

We examine a well-motivated candidate for dark matter derived from a U(1)_{X} extension of the Standard Model, which incorporates a scalar mediator. This dark matter candidate, a Majorana fermion, interacts with the scalar mediator through both the kinetic mixing term and the Higgs sector. Because our model permits complex values for the U(1)_{X} gauge coupling, it supports two distinct dark matter candidates, each with different phenomenological characteristics. Moreover, the scalar mediator's mass relative to the dark matter particle determines a single regime divided into three categories. Consequently, this yields six total configurations that address various detection channels for the scalar mediator. We evaluate its detectability across multiple experimental fronts, including direct searches, colliders, and indirect observations. Through these analyses, we establish comprehensive detection parameter spaces for the scalar mediator by considering various dark matter scenarios.

We demonstrate that for any given dimension $d$ and countable algebraic base field $k$, there exist two isodimensional families: one consisting of $d$-dimensional nilpotent commutative associative $k$-algebras that are irreducible, and another consisting of $d$-dimensional nilpotent commutative associative $k$ algebras whose coordinate rings are smooth points. These findings are published in *Math. Proc. Edinb.* (2020).

Tilted relativistic jets from radio galaxies are often observed to emit radiation in opposite directions on extremely large scales. This work investigates whether the Inverse Compton interaction between these relativistic electrons and Cosmic Microwave Background (CICMB) photons can account for the radiation seen on large scales within Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs). We find that for jets like those in 3C327 and 3C279, the jet beam component involving Landau-Lifshitz (LL) scattering between ultra-relativistic electrons and the CMB photons results in a broad, anisotropic emission profile that spans from UV to X-ray energies. This emission peaks around 10 keV, with a characteristic angular width of approximately 10 relativity radians. Furthermore, the spectral and angular features of this Large-Scale Inverse Compton (LSS-IC) component are sensitive to jet curvature. In scenarios where jets curve on kiloparsec scales, curvature-induced Doppler effects can significantly alter both the emitted spectrum and brightness distribution compared to straight-jet configurations. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of observing this phenomenon through stacked X-ray observations of jet pairs.

We introduce and examine a 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization designed to enable straightforward analytical expansion in the non-relativistic Prandtl-Baker-Holm (PBH) regime for fields and metrics within general relativity. This approach yields analytical expressions for relativistic corrections up to the third post-Prandtl-Baker-Holm (3PB) order for the relativistic potentials—specifically the Birkhoff-Rott functionals—and key observables such as perihelion shift and time dilation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the robustness of this scheme by applying it to the analysis of observables derived from an extended, relativity-compliant Prandtl-Baker-Holm metric.

This paper introduces a robust non-linear image registration approach known as SIFT-CPD, which integrates SIFT feature descriptors with Coupled Point Dynamics (CPD). While standard CPD methods suffer from hyperparameter dependency and limited robustness against contrast variations or local artifacts—common issues in medical imaging—our proposed method overcomes these constraints through the advantages of SIFT features. Empirical evaluations using two datasets, the LITS pneumonectomy dataset and an abdominal CT collection with ground truth labels, confirm that SIFT-CPD achieves superior registration accuracy and robustness compared to existing techniques.

This study introduces the detached eclipsing double-degenerate system SDSS J082239.54$+$304857.19, identified through a high-precision timing analysis of its secondary eclipse. While previously characterized as a double white dwarf system via ground-based photometry, new observations from the K2 mission on board the {\it Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer} (WISE) reveal an additional stellar component, likely a low-mass M dwarf, residing within this binary system.

We investigate the relationship between the host galaxy's spiral structure and the orientation of its Seyfert nuclei. Utilizing data from the ATLAS3D project, we analyzed 30 major-magrite (type 1 and 2) Seyfert galaxies with visible-spectrum polarities to determine their orientations. Our findings indicate a type/spiral structure correlation: spiral hosts of Sa and Sb types host a higher proportion of face-on nuclei for both AGN types, whereas Sd and later spirons predominantly host edge-on nuclei. Additionally, we assessed the potential for both spiral arms and inter-arm regions to influence the orientation distribution of Seyfert nuclei. Our results show that face-on nuclei are more evenly distributed across these regions, while edge-on nuclei are significantly more common in spiral arms than in inter-arms. Finally, we evaluated whether these AGN populations are over-represented in face-on hosts, specifically noting a trend where edge-on nuclei appear disproportionately hosted by bulges with higher specific star formation rates (iFWR).

Existing self-supervised learning approaches typically rely on predicting transformations of image appearances, under the premise that invariant features are captured through these transformations. We challenge this strategy, suggesting that estimating scene geometry is a more robust alternative for pre-training due to the universality of geometric structures. To achieve this, we introduce Monoclass, a self-supervised monocular depth estimation model designed for unstructured scenes. Monoclass utilizes a U-Net architecture and is trained using three loss functions that leverage depth estimates to express image cues including isotropy, continuity, and pixel reconstruction. We assess the approach across various tasks including monocular instance segmentation, detection, and classification on new data sets, as well as transferring to fully supervised and other self-supervised baselines. Experimental results indicate competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art methods, supporting the hypothesis that scene geometry provides a more effective foundation for representing scene structure than traditionally assumed.

This paper examines the status of rare B meson decays and mixing phenomena, focusing on modes like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$, $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$, $\B_s^0\to\pi^\pm\mu^\pm$, and $\B_s^0\to\pi^\pm\mu^\mp$, as well as supersymmetri-related lepton flavor universality tests. We present an examination of theoretical underpinnings, the progress of experimental data, and the implications for physics beyond the Standard Model, concluding with a projection for the future endeavors within this field.

This work examines the one-dimensional Ising model defined on a Cayley tree with branching factor $k$, utilizing a novel group-theoretic methodology. Specifically, the tree's structural properties are encoded within a metacyclic group, which governs an associated unitary representation of an extencinded finitely generated abelian group, providing the primary mathematical framework for further analysis.

This phase-space metric is designed such that its metrics norms precisely quantify the degradation of regularity as smooth solutions to hyperbolic equations evolve into singular ones. Specifically for the three-dimensional Maxwell equations in all but one gauge, this metric serves as the critical threshold: exceeding this mark guarantees the emergence of logarithmic log-log growth.

In 2003, a new approach to Japanese word segmentation utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), a form of recurrent neural network, was introduced alongside a corresponding training dataset. Subsequently in 2005, a robust set of baselines for auto-tagging efficiency was established using a sparse feature vector approach grounded in linguisticality features derived from a vast corpus. Although these baseline systems employed features with high variance, they lacked feature selection mechanisms and feature learning capabilities found in newer techniques. In this study, we revisit these ancient data-driven word-tagging challenges and employ long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks, adapting features originally designed for the historic data sets. Our results reveal a substantial increase in accuracy across the majority of test languages, including Japanese, Chinese, and European languages, surpassing earlier methods by a significant margin.

Stack Overflow (SO) stands as the preeminent community for programmers to seek programming assistance. Although various research efforts have explored leveraging SO's vast repository of knowledge to accelerate code generation through models like stacking, few have examined external resource sharing within the platform itself. This study investigates such sharing behaviors, analyzing the nature, frequency, and underlying motivations of users who distribute outside materials. Key findings include: (1) a skewed distribution where a small cohort accounts for the majority of shared materials, with textbooks receiving the most repeated attention compared to software tools; (2) significant disparities in sharing volumes among individuals holding differing reputation levels, revealing a counterintuitive trend where mid-reputation users surpass high-reputation users in frequency; and (3) a strong correlation between an user's past consumption of specific materials and their likelihood of sharing those same materials, suggesting a motivation rooted in reciprocal benefit. These insights offer critical direction for refining automated support systems and better social engineering strategies.

Observations of approximately 200 nearby galaxies reveal that their rotation curves share a striking universal similarity in the inner regions. To explain this consistency, we investigate whether dark matter (DM) halos possess a universal structural trait. Using $\Lambda$CDM simulations, we demonstrate that this similarity arises because all inner profiles exhibit a flat central core—which we term an "isothermal core"—regardless of total halo mass. This core follows a power-law form, $ \rho(r) = \rho_c (r/r_c)^{-\alpha} $, with characteristic density $\rho_c \simeq 10\,\mathrm{M_\odot\,pc^{-3}}$, scale radius $r_c \simeq 2.5\,\mathrm{kpc}$, and slope $\alpha \simeq 0.3$. Crucially, the diversity seen in outer rotation curves stems from variations in the outer logarithmic slope of the halo, rather than differences in the central core properties. We further establish that this core emerges naturally in $\Lambda$CDM models once the virial radius exceeds $r_c$, a scale set by the universal DM free-streaming length. Consequently, any theoretical model aiming to account for the ubiquity of these inner universal profiles must predict a universal core in its dark matter halo.

Recent evidence indicates that framing climate change personalization around individual values strengthens one's sense of personal responsibility and prompts action. While earlier research has largely concentrated on specific values such as altruism or self-interest, broader motivation theories suggest that connecting alternative value frameworks, like intuition, to climate change may also be effective. This study investigates whether emphasizing personal connections based on intuition fosters consideration of personal impacts and encourages mitigation efforts. Using a randomized experimental design, researchers examined if an intuition-based personalization message outperforms one designed around self-interest. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a message highlighting personal climate change impacts rooted in intuition/self-interest, a self-interest-focused message exclusively, or a control message with no personalization. Results showed that intuition-based personalization equaled or surpassed self-interest-based personalization in encouraging perceived personal responsibility and action,而没有 statistically differing outcomes between the two. However, intuition-only message recipients displayed higher levels of concern regarding climate change more frequently than those exposed to self-interest messages.

This study examines domain generalization techniques applied to healthcare text mining, specifically focusing on extracting signs and symptoms from physician notes. Leveraging extensive datasets composed of thousands of annotated documents collected from diverse institutions, our results demonstrate that employing domain generalization methods enhances sign and symptom extraction performance compared to models trained solely on standard datasets such as BioNLI.

This paper introduces a method for enhancing the trajectory prediction capabilities of autonomous driving systems, specifically targeting scenarios with limited observability. By integrating Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to aggregate temporal information, we contextualize the traditional Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) commonly used in attention mechanisms. Experimental evidence indicates that this proposed approach significantly boosts performance on the widely utilized SOTA framework within the autonomous driving community.

Although neural networks are widely recognized for their superior classification accuracy, their high energy consumption remains a significant limitation. In response, we introduce MQI, a novel spiking neural network designed to rival standard artificial neural networks (ANNs) in classification accuracy while significantly reducing energy usage. Our research demonstrates that MQI is particularly well-suited for periodic tasks, such as classifying images in batch mode. Furthermore, the model exhibits strong potential for integration with Memristive Random Access Memory (MRAM). To validate its efficacy, we evaluated MQI as a general-purpose universal classifier across multiple established datasets. The results show that MQI achieves performance comparable to or exceeding conventional neural networks. Specifically, under MQI, image classification tasks on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10 achieved neuron energy consumptions of approximately 0.02 μJ, 0.03 μJ, and 0.05 μJ per neuron respectively. These dramatic reductions in energy make MQI an ideal choice for applications requiring sustained accuracy with minimal power draw.

We examine the impact of strong magnetic fields on the equation of state of polarized strange quark matter, employing the Bethe–Salpeter equation within the rainbow-ladder approximation. Our findings indicate that both the spin polarization and an external magnetic field strengthen the attraction between quarks, thereby promoting the formation of condensates. However, when evaluating the spin polarization of quark antigauge fields against magnetic contributions to the equation of state, the former proves to be negligible compared to the latter.

To address the limited processing capacity of individual hardware, we introduce Pando, a system enabling collaborative task execution across users' personal devices. Pando matches device capabilities to appropriate computing subtasks, allowing the integration of multiple devices into a unified virtual machine that runs transparently above a user's device fleet. We evaluated Pando using a variety of machine learning models, demonstrating that it can increase data processing rates by 3.7 times compared to single-device execution, at 1.3 to 1.6 times the cost per subtask relative to using one device in isolation.

This paper introduces a novel adaptive sampling technique tailored for finite element approximation of eigenvalues in the Laplace eigenvalue problem. The approach dynamically concentrates sampling points near regions of high gradient within the approximated eigenfunctions. By adaptively guiding the mesh refinement process toward these target areas, the method enhances convergence rates compared to standard uniform sampling strategies. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates the numerical computation of eigenvalues by limiting iterations to eigenfunctions already closely approximated. Evaluation of this technique against well-established finite element results demonstrates both rapid eigenvalue convergence and efficient computational performance.

We investigate the surjectivity of homeomorphisms connecting the survivor sets of various intermediate $\beta$-transformations, with a specific focus on irrational $\beta$ where the corresponding survivor set consists exclusively of badly approximable numbers in a non-integer base. Our findings center on demonstrating both positive and negative instances, with the positive cases driven by new findings concerning the spectral properties of the so-called "golden words."

We investigate how to count quark bilinears that break the $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry in an $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theory with quarks in the vector representation. Because these bilinears transform as the gauge-invariant subset of the fundamental representation, they acquire vacuum expectation values that spontaneously break a portion of the residual chiral symmetry. Our analysis establishes the complete pattern of spontaneous symmetry breaking resulting from these quark bilinears. We confirm these findings using lattice simulations for an $SO(4)$ theory with massless quarks ($N_{c}=N_{F}=2$), which exhibits chiral symmetry breaking in the pattern $SU(2)\times SU(2) \to SU(2)_{\text{diag}}$. Furthermore, simulations for the $SU(N_{c})$ with fundamental matter analogs—specifically an $SO(4)$ theory $N_{c}=3$ quarks—showed that the pattern of symmetry breaking is consistent with our theoretical predictions.

Many real-world challenges involve predicting a target variable based on a set of curves, where each data point is actually a time-series itself. Although deep learning methods have excelled in curve forecasting, they typically function as "black boxes," making it difficult to comprehend the underlying mechanisms of their predictions. This paper addresses this limitation by introducing a method that simultaneously enhances accuracy and transparency through "Disentangled Attribution Curves." Unlike standard approaches that focus on single values, our technique disintegrates each input curve into distinct temporal trends, such as daily or periodic patterns, and subsequently generates attribution curves to reveal their influence on the forecast. We validated our approach against two public bike-sharing datasets, where it outperformed baseline models and offered insightful revelations into the features driving its predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrated the method's versatility across various applications, including forecasting the evolution of COVID-19.

This study introduces Privacy-Safe Federative Learning (PSFL), a privacy-secured method enabling clients to collaboratively train a model with a shared understanding, while mitigating the risks of data leakage. Conventional privacy techniques suffer from significant drawbacks, including prohibitively high computational costs, compromised accuracy, and the necessity for pre-existing trust among participants. In contrast, the proposed approach offers superior time and memory efficiency alongside enhanced results. By integrating this framework, clients can engage in federated learning without establishing prior trust with others while ensuring their data remains secure.

This document outlines a solution for microcontroller-based drivers validation, designed to augment existing on-chip Single Cycle Cell TLM (SCC-TLM) cores. By integrating two non-intrusive circuits with SCC-TLM to facilitate memory read and write operations, the approach enables comprehensive off-line driver testing on microcontrollers. This methodology supports multiple microcontrollers, including those featuring built-in Test-Logic-Enhanced (LTE) features. The paper presents validation results confirming the methodology's effectiveness.

"Hardware support for filtering system calls is essential for numerous applications, including remote procedure call mechanisms and hardware-assisted virtualization. Although recent systems (e.g., Intel's UProbes and AMD's secure microcode) offer this capability for compiled programs, applications written in interpreted languages such as PHP and Python currently lack it. We introduce *Timeloops*, a novel system call filtering solution for remote procedures and other hardware virtualization solutions. Timeloops achieves this by runtime analyzing call patterns to identify and filter system calls specific to the running application, a process performed without requiring prior knowledge or setup. Specifically, it utilizes time-bound loops executed within a runtime profiler to observe and analyze specific call patterns, a method applicable to both compiled and interpreted applications. During this process, Timeloops simultaneously constructs a white-list of allowed systems calls and integrates it into existing systems seamlessly, providing both functionality and transparency to users."

Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis faces significant hurdles due to high dimensionality, complex interactions between dimensions, and the scarcity of labels. To address these labeling challenges, we propose a framework for classifying high-dimensional data in low-dimensional product space forms. This approach maps raw data, modeled as a product space, onto structured combinations of lower-dimensional subspaces. We introduce a step-by-step algorithm to classify scRNA-seq data into these forms using only summary statistics, specifically the counts matrix. Our results indicate that this method yields a classification performance improvement of up to 20% compared to Euclidean spaces. Furthermore, the technique demonstrates substantial gains in handling high-dimensional scRNA-seq data by constraining it within a structured product space during analysis. We have made our computational tools freely available on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/AmirhosseiniLab/ProductSpace.

This study investigates how a supermassive black hole (SMBH) influences stellar scattering within its surrounding cluster. We developed an analytical framework to compute the modification induced by an SMBH on the scattering of incoming stars—possoting orbital energies significantly higher than the local cluster values—towards energy levels typical of the cluster environment. The analysis relies on approximations of both the cluster's mass function and its one-body distribution regarding orbital energies and angular momenta. We demonstrate that, even for angular momenta well above the critical threshold for capture, the scattering cross-section can be enhanced by orders of magnitude when the cluster's mass function follows a power law with an index below -1.5. Furthermore, we extend this analysis to explore the impact of angular momentum distribution on the scattering process.

Stochastic Model Predictive Control (MPC) manages system uncertainty by recalcitrating control actions as uncertainty evolves; however, practical limitations often prevent real-time uncertainty assessment, necessitating its offline approximation. While offline approximation is standard, it typically sacrifices control performance to ensure feasible implementations. This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing neural networks for the offline approximation of uncertainty and enables the enhancement of one specific optimization scenario within each individual MPC horizon through an optimization-based update every single step. The study demonstrates through one typical case and two real-world applications, including an unmanned underwater vehicle and a wind turbine control system, that the neural-network MPC framework allows for better performance compared to existing offline approaches, while maintaining reasonable computational costs for implementation.

This paper addresses independent component analysis (ICA) in a compressed setting, introducing two new algorithms that are memory-efficient alternatives to existing approaches. Our primary contributions include the Compressive ICA algorithm, which enables the reconstruction of full-dimensional data from a reduced set of measurements by leveraging a specific class of mixtures, and a more general Compressive Nonlinear ICA designed for scenarios where data exists in its compressed form. Experimental results demonstrate that these methods achieve accurate recovery with high precision, outperforming established baseline techniques regarding computational overhead. Both approaches are theoretically grounded in the Johnson-Ahlswede-Alon framework and include detailed explanations of their procedural steps.

We introduce a variant of the asymmetric noisy voter model involving two competing species, characterized by local majority rule bias and random noise. This framework investigates the dynamical consequences of imbalances between random noise and biased preferential voting when applied to two distinct spatial configurations: a finite line segment and an infinite binary tree. Our findings demonstrate that on both domains, the competition between these two species results in three potential outcomes: the complete fixation of one species (fixation), the perpetual coexistence of both (coexistence), or a mosaic state involving domains of both (mixture). This work establishes that both mixture and coexistence behaviors represent novel phenomena within the study of voter model competitions. We further derive sufficient conditions regarding the parameters that determine which of the three regimes will occur. Notably, the conditions required to reach a mixture or coexistence differ between the interval and the tree topologies, with the tree presenting a more favorable environment for establishing such behaviors than an interval does.

This work examines a photonic quantum photo-detector array coupled coherently through a feedback loop, focusing on in-plane cavity arrangements capable of generating multimer entanglement. Notably, this coherent coupling provides robust protection against thermal entanglement. Consequently, the system can produce purely photonic entanglement even under strong thermal conditions. Our findings are substantiated by quantitative robustity comparisons and Robustness Quantifiers (RQ). Additionally, we explore how coherent feedback influences the Gibbs state of open quantum systems, suggesting that such loops could replace conventional quantum control techniques.

Alongside historical dials, contemporary examples continue to be erected; specifically, the initiative to document these modern pieces began in 2021 by forming a WhatsApp group for Indonesian sun dials. As an example, we have developed a graphical user interface (GUI) enabling the graphical control of polarimetric measurements within an astrometry laboratory setting. This system is built atop a software framework capable of managing any graphical interface, sensor data acquisition, communications protocols, and magnetic field generation interfaces. Spherical electrostatic phase plates (EEPPs) play a pivotal role in advancing transmission electron microscopy (TEM) capabilities by enhancing contrast through phase contrast techniques. As TEMs with EEPS achieve higher resolutions in line with advancing technology, simulations have become indispensable for optimizing performance and designing novel plates. This study employs multiparticle tracking simulations to analyze how EEPS architecture influences electron probe characteristics, specifically probe size and current density. Specific attention is given to the fill-factor and pixel configurations on plates featuring hexagonal patterns with copper profiles. Furthermore, multiprobe scanning simulations were conducted to evaluate how probe attributes affect image resolution, resulting in contrast transfer function (CTF) analyses that reveal distinct periodicity based on pixel arrangement and demonstrate the trade-off between contrast and resolution dictated by the probe size. Ultimately, these findings provide critical insights for constructing effective phase plates and advancing TEM applications.

This article proposes a comprehensive theory linking the physics of computation across various physical substrates to cognitive processes. Combinations of computationally simple interactions across different computation types drive both physical computing mechanisms and the computational capabilities inherent in minds. Within this theoretical framework, however, quantum computation stands apart; it lacks an direct analog in other physical realization methods and therefore requires a separate consideration regarding its specific characteristics and theoretical implications for wider computational systems and intelligence.

Recent efforts have explored the concept of quantum entanglement as a mechanism for constructing bridges between spacetime regions, an hypothesis formally outlined by the ER=EPR conjecture. While significant theoretical progress has been made, a standard model for these structures remains elusive. Addressing a specific instance from a recent study, this paper compares polymer black holes and wormholes designed with analogous attributes, focusing on their quasi-local energy, causal geometry, and asymptotic symmetries to evaluate their structural integrity. Our findings indicate an unexpected correspondence between the two solutions despite their distinct natures: a wormhole satisfies the Null Energy Condition (NEC) and exhibits anti-de Sitter-like asymptotic geometry, whereas a black hole violates the NEC and adopts asymptotic similarities to Schwarzschild spacetime. Nevertheless, the two are related through a duality wherein their energy profiles and asymptotic boundaries are essentially duals, and both possess equal cardinalities of degrees of freedom. These insights offer a novel perspective on quantizing gravity within isolated systems.

We conducted numerical renormalization group calculations on an effective Hamiltonian representing the singlet pairing gapless Green's function of doped graphene sheets, where electron-electron interactions are present alongside spin-flip interactions derived from the Kondo model. This numerical approach enabled the electron-specific heat analysis and revealed a linear temperature dependence at low temperatures, governed by a velocity constant determined through the renormalization of the quasiparticle speed. Consequently, this linear term in specific heat signifies that, within this effective theoretical framework, contributions from electrons compete with those from magnetic spin excitations, rather than being exclusively dominated by one source.

We introduce a novel end-to-end system, named MaskedSpeech, for natural and expressive speech synthesis that leverages a mask-based approach. This framework employs a speech-specific masked auto-encoder to learn a latent representation capable of capturing details vital for speech quality. A conditional flow-based autoregressive model then generates the latent space sequentially to facilitate high-fidelity speech reconstruction using an explicit speech prior for naturalness and a prosody model for controlled expressivity. Our proposed speech-focused architecture outperforms existing methods established by the Espanso et al. (2020) baseline on the Librispeech test set with a clean hold-out strategy, achieving 2.11 bits per speech sample—significantly lower than 2.19 bits per speech sample—previously recorded by Espanso et al. (2). We provide code and models available at https://github.com/IEIT-CNRN/MaskedSpeech.

This study introduces a robust permutation test framework for multivariate post-selection inference in Bayesian Lasso regression. Unlike conventional methods that may discard unique uncertainty characteristics from the original model, our approach preserves the posterior uncertainties inherent in the prior distribution. By employing this test to evaluate a graph-guided genomic selection method within a case-control framework, we identify informative gene sets associated with various diseases. Consequently, we offer robust uncertainty estimates regarding the significance of these identified gene associations.

Recent studies have demonstrated that adversaries can manipulate neural network outputs by introducing carefully crafted perturbations undetected by humans. Building on this, we investigate how an adversary possessing only a single pixel modification capability can execute a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack against deep learning models. Our proposed approach transfers the adversarial example from the source model to the target through a stealthy keyboard stroke on a virtual keyboard, effectively bypassing both anti-forensics defenses and requiring only access to the audio frequency response of a speaker system. This single stroke transfers the perturbed input from the speaker to the user's microphone, then wire transmission to the target model on the server side, resulting in 90% classification accuracy across multiple benchmarks such as CNNs and RNNs for image recognition tasks. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in multi-user and multi-device scenarios without losing effectiveness.

This research examines the propagation pathways of conspiracy theory-driven climate change misinformation within social media networks. By applying network clustering techniques and content analysis, our study investigates how these networks propagate. Specifically, we analyzed over 150,000 tweets discussing conspiracy theory-based climate change topics to explore their diffusion patterns. Our findings indicate that isolated micro-blogs serve as the primary source distributing these falsehoods. Furthermore, we observed that recipients within social media communities exhibit limited capacity to distinguish credible from unreliable content. These results underscore the critical need for targeted communication strategies aimed at susceptible individuals to enhance resilience against such misinformation.

This study presents an examination of dark matter interactions occurring at multi-TeV energy scales, utilizing a data set of 140 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the ATLAS detector at the CERN Large Hadron Collider during proton-proton collisions at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. The analysis targets single-tagged events featuring at least one lepton, significant missing transverse momentum, and a jet with high momentum. Our findings align with Standard Model predictions, showing no statistical anomaly. These results, therefore, exclude certain theoretical models proposed within simplified dark matter frameworks. Specifically, for a scenario involving the interaction of a single vector mediator with quarks, 95\% confidence level limits on the product of the branching fraction and cross-section are established in the range of 0.1–1.0 fb across a mediator mass spectrum from 1.2 to 14.5 TeV. Additionally, these findings constrain various simplified dark matter topologies, as well as the universal extra dimensions model featuring Kaluza-Klein bulk neutrons decaying into Standard Model baryons and leptons.

Exangulated categories serve as a generalization of both exact and Frobenius exact categories, a framework developed by Liu and Zhang based on the notion of weakly closed splitting-exangulated categories introduced independently by Chen and Zhang. In this article, we investigate homological properties within such weakly closed splitting-exangulated categories, establishing a criterion for their existence based on an equivalent condition relating to the Serre duality. Furthermore, we examine how certain constructions, including pullbacks and pushforuts, interact with exangles derived from these categories.

This paper provides a comparative analysis of the earnings returns to post-secondary skills in Norway versus Denmark, utilizing recent data from both nations to evaluate the effectiveness of their educational systems in preparing students for the labor market. By merging linked employer-employee surveys and tax records, we conduct an analysis at the field of study level that surpasses previous cross-country educational comparisons in granularity. We find that while the pattern of earnings returns to fields of study is largely consistent between the two countries, the overall earnings level per field is significantly higher in Norway than in Denmark. Furthermore, the analysis highlights that post-secondary education in Norway serves as a more specialized mechanism for acquiring job-specific human capital, particularly evident in fields such as nursing and within the broader category of technical post-secondary education.

The BEPCII electron-positron collider operating at the Super $J/\psi$ energy scale offers access to a high accumulation of data around physical parameters like the $\tau$ decay properties and the masses and mixing parameters of $B$-mesons. This abundance of data opens up fresh avenues for B-physics and anomalous $\tau$ decay investigations. The article provides a comprehensive overview of the current status and achievements of research programs at BEPCII.

Gravitational lenses that arise from hierarchical multi-star systems offer valuable insights into the formation and evolution of these systems. This study examines the accretion dynamics of binary systems embedded within a three-star configuration, where the hierarchical scale is much larger than the separation between the inner pair ("binary + companion"), and demonstrates that the material accreted by the smaller component behaves similarly to that accreted by a single star of equivalent mass. Consequently, this observation implies that the conclusion drawn from the first author's work—that the first member of a lenticular binary cannot sustain a classical T Tauri phase—is valid regardless of the system's specific topology.

The piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model enables the segmentation of damaged images by enforcing constant regions and limiting discontinuities in edges, yet it often fails to preserve sharp boundaries within homogeneous areas due to smoothing effects caused by its variational formulation. Although sharp variations can be achieved through regularization refinement, these variants remain confined to image domains, excluding valuable external information. In this work, we incorporate a prior knowledge of regularity outside the target domain into the model to enhance these homogeneous zones. By merging this external prior with the classical approach in a variational framework, we define an optimization problem that yields a Mumford-Shah-type functional featuring a regularization term with Lipschitz continuity. To resolve this problem efficiently, we employ a new approximation of Lipschitz regularization that facilitates a simplified variational structure compatible with efficient solving methods, such as an alternate variational approach combined with a fast scheme tailored to the regularization component. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that this proposed model achieves performance on par with refined sharp-edge versions while producing qualitative improvements via edge preservation and uniform region reconstruction.

Recent years have seen significant experimental efforts to search for ultra-light particles and the signals they generate; however, the lack of conclusive results has prompted calls for broader theoretical exploration of these phenomena. This paper examines the concept of on-chip learning within neuromorphic computing and its implications for designing efficient neurosynaptic arrays. Unlike traditional approaches where learning methods are fixed by manufactured hardware parameters, neumorphonic computing enables weights and thresholds to be dynamically updated through online plasticity mechanisms. This paradigm shift opens up new research avenues for developing online learning algorithms tailored for VLSI implementation on neuromorphic processors. This framework also establishes benchmark metrics to assess and compare various computational approaches. Specifically, the work focuses on clustering as a representative task. We demonstrate a planar-integrated miniature optical lattice configuration that significantly enhances the transfer efficiency from a MOT to a one-dimensional linear trap, simplifying fabrication and reducing space requirements. By planar-integrating the $\Lambda$-type trap within the MOT chamber, we achieve rapid atom transfer with peak efficiencies reaching approximately 50%. This approach facilitates the compact miniaturization of entire optical atomic clock systems, supporting integration with photonic structures and on-chip detection.

The identification of M82* and M8M's low luminosity presents a significant observational challenge. In this study, we propose a model in which a dense cluster, specifically a cluster of massive compact objects (MCOs), forms in the central region of the galaxy's accretion disk. These objects include stellar-mass black holes, neutron stars, and black holes with intermediate mass. We further demonstrate that this dense MCO cluster can effectively clear a surrounding cavity in the accretion disk, a process that accounts for the object's suppressed luminosity. Additionally, we analyze the characteristics of radiation emitted by this unique cluster of MCOs.

We conduct an analysis of a neutral atom moving along the axis of a mirror, focusing on how its quantum and classical states couple with an electromagnetic field. Using input-output framework combined with a master equation, we explore photon emission resulting from both excited and ground state atoms interacting with a mirror, noting that these processes arise from both stimulated and spontaneous scattering. Our findings extend beyond the conventional Jaynes-Cummings model for static atoms to encompass the influence of translational motion. We demonstrate that for a classical atom undergoing harmonic oscillation, coherent states are preserved throughout the interaction. Furthermore, we investigate specific quantum scenarios involving emission from a two-level atom in its lower state as well as spontaneous or stimulated decay from an excited state, with particular attention to how quantum fluctuations in atomic position and momentum impact these processes.

We utilize a dynamical agent-based simulation to analyze the young massive cluster Westerlund 2 (WLu 2), leveraging its well-constrained physical characteristics. Our findings reveal that massive-star ejection occurs in approximately 20% of cases, with a mean post-ejection velocity of 9 km/s—a figure comparable to velocity dispersion measurements derived from optical data. Consequently, we estimate that about 20% of massive stars form within a dynamical radius of 2.5 pc, an area that encompasses the observed cluster. Our results further indicate that for clusters with a power-law high-mass slope index $\alpha \gtrsim 2.2$, massive stars are predominantly ejected during dynamical interactions with other massive objects rather than through two-body relaxation. In these regimes, nearly all ejectees originate from direct exchanges involving binary systems or direct collisions. Conversely, in clusters characterized by a flattened mass distribution ($\alpha < 2.2$), dynamical friction becomes the primary mechanism for massive star ejection, allowing us to confirm that most ejectees remain outside the observed radius of 2.5 pc. Collectively, these findings suggest that a universal structural profile for massive clusters cannot be assumed; rather, dynamical evolutions are dictated by initial conditions, specifically the mass slope and saturation level of dynamical saturation.

This study aims to establish a variational framework for finding strong solutions to the constant coefficient incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^n$. By applying the minimax principle to an appropriately defined vector field, the demonstration begins with the guarantee of a solution to a variational problem. subsequently, it is proven that this solution satisfies the strong Navier-Stokes equations within a specific function space for at least some initial time. Notably, this approach does not rely on smallness conditions—neither on the size of the data nor its size—and thus applies to both finite and constant support scenarios.

While integrating handwritten text recognizers with degraded document image enhancement networks can improve recognition outcomes, achieving task-specific image restoration through unsupervised GANs alone is often insufficient. To address limitations in reconstruction fidelity, this work introduces a fine-tuning approach using StyleGAN2 as a generative prior within a GANs-NICE (Gradient-NICe) framework to synthesize high-quality examples. Evaluation against other enhancement techniques and integration into a recognizer pipeline demonstrate improved character quality and details in degraded documents, validating the approach for creating clearer images that aid text recognition.

Leveraging Natural Language Processing (NLP), we built a specialized algorithm to extract textual data from various forms of Indonesian National Identity Cards. By analyzing layout patterns and applying linguistic tags, we successfully developed this system, achieving an average text extraction accuracy of 98.68%.

This paper introduces a novel deep learning approach for channel estimation in high-mobility scenarios, leveraging long short term memory (LSTM) networks to mitigate rapid channel variations through their unique temporal dependencies. To enhance efficiency by reducing inference latency, the proposed structure employs a partitioned training methodology for LSTM. Additionally, the technique utilizes a dedicated data preprocessing stage to extract channel characteristics, thereby lowering model complexity. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that this method surpasses prior state-of-the-art results, particularly in terms of partitioned training efficacy.

Deep learning techniques offer powerful solutions for various difficult tasks, including super-resolution. This paper presents a solution for improving the clarity of low-resolution astrophysical spectra, a process known as spectral deconvolution or super-resolution. The approach combines a custom loss function with a new resolution kernel designed to significantly improve observed data quality. By integrating this method into the super-fast on-spectroscopy reduction pipeline, researchers can efficiently generate high-resolution spectra for numerous transient astronomical events without delay.

This study introduces an algorithm designed to infer a neural network by emulating a probabilistic programming model. To avoid overfitting to the training data without relying on standard regularization techniques or manual hyperparameter tuning, the method alternates between neural network optimization and a Bayesian Gaussian process interpolation over training inputs. This interpolation approximates a neural network with a closed-form posterior distribution, enabling efficient marginalization to approximate Bayesian neural networks (BANNs). The algorithm's contributions are validated against existing algorithms for BANNs invariance testing, demonstrating superior performance on synthetic datasets comparable to grid-based methods, while significantly outperforming grid-based approaches in terms of computational efficiency.

The European Collider Physics Fair's Early Career Researcher (ECFCER) was founded in 2016, marking its formal start in 2018 following a name change from its predecessor. We introduce an all-optical line wave propagator utilizing a graphene layer situated within a dielectric waveguide. By employing the Langmuir model for optical energies, we demonstrate that an elliptically patterned graphene region serves as a line wave generator. Conversely, an elliptically designed isolated strip of graphene functioning as an aperture acts as the source for these line waves. Our findings indicate that the system's geometry governs the propagation of line waves, with light confinement achieved through the surface plasmon resonance of the graphene strips. These line waves can interact selectively with optical defects positioned at the focal points of the design. This mechanism offers promising applications in the fields of plasmonics and photonics, particularly for developing all-optical components such as beam deflection systems, optical switches, and sensors based on line wave interactions.

We introduce a framework for collaboratively learning complex multi-agent interactions involving multiple humans and robots, grounded in the Federated Learning (FL) paradigm. Conventional reinforcement learning methods struggle with such scenarios due to the expansive state-action spaces resulting in prohibitively large parameter sets, making them unsuitable for scalable collaboration. By leveraging FL, our approach enables a group of interacting humans and robots to jointly develop shared understanding of the environment and interaction patterns, including personal models tailored to individual humans and central models for the robotic ensemble. Each human interacts with a personal model to guide the robot, while the collective ensemble refines its central model through these interactions, all within a private data context. This ensures data privacy by preventing the centralization of information, which mitigates biases and enhances the generalizability of the learned policies. We validate this FL-based methodology for modeling human-robot and human-human interactions within a virtual setting, demonstrating its efficacy in scenarios where the underlying interaction mechanics remain unknown.

A smooth-completeness bias-reduced estimator is proposed in this paper that achieves asymptotic smoothness in terms of bias. The algorithm exhibits optimal performance in terms of the benchmark problem's estimation error, as measured by the L2 norm, up to log factors. The study further highlights the algorithm's performance against state-of-the-art alternatives, as measured by prediction and treatment effect estimation errors, as demonstrated in a comprehensive simulation study.

Although the method's outflow relevance is nearly consistent, its input-side relevance can vary depending on the specific LRP variant employed. We introduce a generalized form of the parameter $m$ associated Stirling numbers of the second kind, defined as $m$-associated Stirling numbers by replacing the finite power of the base polynomial with a specific combinatorial structure that ensures the extended relationship holds for various integers $m$. This redefinition covers both lower and upper variants, along with corresponding factorial definitions, extending existing combinatorial families to a broader scope by allowing $m$ to vary. Furthermore, we explore a polynomial connection between these generalized entities and the standard binomial coefficients, establishing recurrences that include dual formulations to streamline computation for various problems. Their application extends to encoding specific types of cyclic arrangements where no consecutive run exceeds a limit determined by $m$, thereby providing a novel combinatorial interpretation. This interpretation allows us to derive fresh interpretations of previously known combinatorial identities, including generalized versions of the Newton forward difference formula, binomial coefficient expansion theorems, and other fundamental algebraic relations. Finally, we demonstrate that our results unify several existing combinatorial expansions, showing they all emerge naturally from this broader framework.

Irreducible domains, representing regions of distinct symmetry within a parent symmetry that are separated by domain walls, have gained significant attention across physics and chemistry due to their potential to host novel states of matter. This interest stems from their ability to interact with external fields, allowing for precise control over irreducible domains. A primary obstacle to research and application remains a knowledge gap regarding their dimensions and orientations. This study addresses that challenge by introducing a framework for classifying and predicting irreducible domains, specifically within 2D layered materials exhibiting low-symmetry point groups. The findings demonstrate that irreducible domains, defined by specific crystallographic planes, align with symmetry operations and correspond to distinct symmetry-adapted orders defined by that specific domain. The proposed model offers a valuable tool for investigating tunable ferroic responses in 2D ferroelectrics and ferromagnets and related phenomena within analogous 2D and 3D materials.

We present a framework for the quark mass matrix based on a flavor U(1)$_F$ symmetry breaking mechanism, utilizing a superpotential that accommodates a general mass matrix structure. By employing a slanted superpotential formulation, the model yields an approximate mass hierarchy where m$_t$ >> m$_b$, effectively distinguishing the top quark's dominance over bottom quarks. While charged flavor observables remain consistent with experimental bounds, the framework successfully reproduces the charged scalar mass spectrum, thereby providing a compelling rationale for the existence of a lightest neutral scalar with m$_{h1} = 125$ GeV.

Virtual Platform Performance Monitoring Units (VPPMs) enable cross-processor performance observation and tracing across a Manycore system via paritualization techniques like Multi-Processing Environment Transport (MET). While beneficial, their potential malevolent application poses significant risks, such as tracking process behavior, gathering process-related information, or spying on sensitive data through a victim process's cache line activity. To mitigate these threats, this paper proposes VPPM-safe Secure Execution (SAFE-VPP), a hardware and software framework designed to hinder unauthorized monitoring and data theft using illegal VPPM activities. SAFE-VPP utilizes Secure Execution Regions (SERs), a hardware feature that isolates sensitive processes and shields them from unauthorized observation, alongside multi-level permission control to restrict VPPM access based on different privilege levels, thereby ensuring secure and controlled performance monitoring in many-core environments.

The rise of pre-trained language models has enabled significant advancements in natural language processing for established languages, yet their cross-lingual capabilities—particularly regarding low-resource languages—are under-researched. This study addresses two critical inquiries: first, why do these models struggle to adapt to new languages, particularly those with limited data, and second, which architectural designs offer the greatest flexibility. To explore these issues, we conduct zero-shot prompting experiments on four distinct prompt engineering tasks across twenty diverse languages. Our findings reveal that pre-trained models exhibit substantial performance disparities when moving from high-resource to low-resource environments, with the latter showing particularly poor results. By correlating zero-shot performance with various textual and semantic attributes of these languages, we identify specific factors governing their adaptability. Furthermore, we compare performance across different prompt architectures to determine which lever is architecturally superior. To mitigate the challenges identified, we introduce PromptSLT—a universal model pre-trained on UDC299—a multilingual corpus comprising 299 diverse texts. Our results demonstrate that this approach significantly enhances adaptability, especially in scenarios with scant linguistic resources.

Comprehending the narratives shaping public discourse on social platforms is essential for informing debates, particularly as these narratives often undergo shifts in polarity over time. To address this, we introduce **Narrative Tracking (NT)**, a novel network-based methodology designed to monitor narratives within Twitter networks. This approach captures both narratives and their connections, facilitating the examination of their interactions. We outline the network structures relevant to this proposal, present **narrative extraction algorithms** to identify relevant content, and implement **narrative and connection tagging procedures**. By applying this framework to the Twitter discussions surrounding **Brexit**, the study maps the networks of distinct narratives, analyzes their interactions, and investigates the networks' structural connections through **centrality metrics**, **clustering coefficients**, and **network visualization**. Furthermore, we assess how networks of opposing narratives evolve by examining **network density**, **assortativity**, and **narrative polarity shifts**. Ultimately, these tools provide the means to network analysis, enabling researchers to investigate narratives and their interactions on Twitter for informed decision-making regarding public policy and social issues.

Detecting occurrences of significance within video streams is vital for numerous real-world applications. While existing systems primarily rely on deep learning to classify events or actions utilizing fixed, rigid grid structures, this paper introduces a novel framework for a spatio-temporal event detection process that accommodates events varying spatially. This method employs a hierarchical approach, beginning with a coarsely defined feature space, to efficiently filter out irrelevant areas, thereby concentrating computational resources on event-rich zones while maintaining high precision. Our proposed architecture integrates spatial pooling, temporal modeling, and adaptive detection mechanisms. Specifically, it relies on a Coarsened Feature Map (CFM) that matches each detected event with its corresponding coarse grid, followed by a Hierarchical Event Detection (HiED) step that identifies potential event locations. Complementing this is a Spatial Feature Enhancement (SFE) module, which boosts the signal-to-noise ratio by refining event boundaries via a dedicated segmentation head. Extensive evaluations on benchmark datasets—including ME-Dataset, UCF-Video Qu-Qu, UCF-NUT, and UCF-101—demonstrate that this method surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions.

We introduce a framework designed to train deep neural networks with guaranteed robustness against worst-case perturbations, assuming an accurate approximation of the uncertainty distribution of adversarial disturbances. By leveraging a generative adversarial network, this distribution is sampled, subsequently transforming the original stochastic optimization task into a constrained non-linear programming problem. The solution to these constraints is obtained via a direct method utilizing a reformulation approach within the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) paradigm. Empirical evaluations on various deep learning architectures demonstrate that the resulting models exhibit enhanced robustness against both state-of-the-art adversarial attacks and theoretical adversarial examples, all without compromising accuracy.

Rumor attenuation is a critical challenge within the field of social network analysis. While many existing approaches focus on identifying and removing influential rumors to lower dissemination volume, these methods often fail to address the core issue: reducing the peak height of the rumor curve. This study introduces a novel learning-based model designed specifically to minimize rumor peaks by simultaneously leveraging historical data on rumour features and geographical context. The model employs the Long Short-Term Network (LSTM) framework, enhanced by the inclusion of both precursor rumour indicators and location data, which significantly advances prediction accuracy. Furthermore, we developed an optimization technique for the rumor's attenuation coefficient, designed to achieve rapid convergence and high precision when paired with peak prediction models. Empirical results indicate that our proposed model consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art methodologies in rumor attenuation prediction.

Hyperspectral image (HSI) pixel classification is essential across numerous fields, yet the massive nature of HSI samples typically necessitates the extensive utilization of signature datasets. This dependency leads to significant computational overhead and a decline in classification efficiency. While dimensionality reduction techniques (DRTs) have emerged as a potential solution, most are specialized for specific tasks, and many fail to effectively exploit the spatial characteristics of HSI. This research introduces a novel DRT named Spatial-Adaptive Local Linear Regression (SALLLR), designed to enhance both signal reconstruction capabilities and the computational efficiency of pixel classification. SALLLR initially leverages local linear regression to adaptively identify optimal source pixels for a given test pixel, subsequently employing the local structure of the HSI to reconstruct the target using regression based on these selected samples. Following a comprehensive evaluation across multiple benchmark datasets, the study confirms that SALLLR not only surpasses conventional dimensionality reduction techniques in signal reconstruction but also delivers a considerable reduction in processing time.

Compressing Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) has become a critical area of study, with applications ranging from accelerating inference on embedded devices to enhancing model robustness against poisoning and adversarial attacks. Although recent advancements have enabled significant real-world applications, many techniques depend heavily on extensive agent training, which incurs considerable computational costs. Although intrinsic motivation was previously introduced to reinforce learning by providing additional learning signals, its effectiveness remains limited due to the standard practice of overwhelming motivation with large amounts of extrinsic reward data during training. This study demonstrates that properly balancing both reward sources can substantially accelerate training in reinforcement learning agents. Our results indicate that leveraging a combination of intrinsic motivation and extrinsic rewards significantly improves learning outcomes, particularly in scenarios involving sparse reward conditions. Consequently, this approach leads to superior agent performance and markedly reduces training efficiency in terms of computational requirements.

This work extends our earlier investigation (arXiv:2012.09094) into the connected domain of the coloured Poincaré group, a framework capable unifying various calibrated Minkowski symmetries. We introduce a distinct, integrable model incorporating both massive and massless particles governed by this coloured algebra. Furthermore, our current research expands upon various integrable systems derived from this structure, particularly in the context of black hole spacetimes defined by the Kerr metric. We also outline several applications relative to integrable models situated within both the coloured Poincaré group and its corresponding massive/massless representations.

We suggest employing tree-width as a foundational concept for understanding "directed acyclic graph treewidth." This paper examines how this parameter influences and applies to algorithmic techniques directed at DAGs.

This study introduces MemoNav, a memory-based navigational modeling framework designed specifically to address multi-destination scenarios. The model utilizes an ego-centric GAD (Global Attention Decoder for Navigation) mechanism to estimate future movement trajectories, which are guided by a self-generated memory map. In this memory map, previously visited locations are marked to allow the encoder to aggregate information about them. Subsequently, the ego-centric GAD refines its navigation via an attention mechanism focused on these remembered paths, enabling the simulation of multiple navigation tasks while being influenced by past behavior. We evaluated the model on two real-world datasets, WayUp and NGSIM, comparing it against state-of-the-art baselines. Results demonstrate that MemoNav achieves superior navigational performance over previous methods on both datasets. Furthermore, when navigating multiple targets simultaneously within a single trajectory, the model shows a 30% average improvement in edge F-score compared to standard single-task models.

Wireless communication technology continues to evolve rapidly, progressing from 4G to 5G New Radio (NR), with wireless 6 (6G) serving as its subsequent sixth generation. As non-licensed bands like the 6GHz range become integral to 6G, understanding and enhancing interference mitigation techniques within these frequencies is vital for robust communication. This paper presents a new interference mitigation strategy designed specifically for the 6GHz band, designed to offer a more efficient and optimized approach by providing better coverage and reduced interference compared to existing methods. This method employs a MIMO system with a base station utilizing intelligent meta-surface metasurface (IMM). Furthermore, this paper also presents a proposed optimization algorithm to enhance the total system spectral efficiency (tSE). This new approach combines the advantages of total variation (TV) regularization with the Sequential Linear Programming (SLP) method. By utilizing TV-regularization, this approach optimizes the total transmit power by reducing it significantly, leading to improved performance outcomes when compared to existing algorithms.

This study examines the existence of steady-state solutions in population density models featuring space O(n) symmetry, incorporating non-local mean field interactions and diffusive mechanisms. These symmetries commonly emerge from coarse-graining procedures in lattice-based models. Our methodology involves demonstrating that specific values of a symmetry-breaking parameter, coupled with strong long-range interactions and diffusive coupling tailored to a particular wave number, yield asymptotic solutions in the form of periodic functions or Turing patterns. This finding generalizes previous results regarding asymmetric cases ($n=1$) to broader scenarios. This approach provides additional theoretical backing for observed spatial heterogeneity in biological aggregations, such as zebrafish schooling and mouse social interactions.

This work examines the initiation and propagation of cracks in brittle materials featuring a characteristic length scale, such as quasi-brittle materials, which exhibit process zones at the crack tip. Employing a cohesive zone model, we analyze the relationship between intrinsic length scales and high-loading crack initiation thresholds. Our findings, derived from a finite element framework, contrast energy release rates and maximum tensile stresses to explore Low-Loading (LE) regimes and High-Stress (HS) regimes. In the LE regime, we apply Linear Elastic Fracture Mechanics (LEFM) to predict crack initiation using either the maximum principal stress or an energy density criterion. Conversely, within the HS regime we adopt Fracture Mechanics (LEFM) and evaluate crack initiation via a maximum principal stress approach. Our results confirm a direct correlation between the material's inherent scale and stress levels required to trigger cracking under intense loading conditions. Specifically, we validate that both LE predictions—whether based on stress criteria or energy considerations—accurately forecast cracking in the LE scenario. Similarly, FRM predictions effectively address cracking when loading is significant. Ultimately, we propose a generalizable framework for predicting crack initiation across varying stress environments, applicable to a diverse range of quasi-brittle materials.
