This paper introduces a new bio-inspired climbing robot named Trident, designed to climb vertical glass surfaces using suction cups as its attachment mechanism. Driven by a combination of undulatory body movements and suction cup deployment/retraction, Trident demonstrated significant advancements in both speed and load-bearing capacity compared to its predecessors. Specifically, it achieved a vertical ascent speed of 1.7 body lengths per second (bps) while supporting a payload equivalent to 0.42 of its own body weight (1.7 LW). As a result, Trident outperforms the Pacific Lamprey—the traditional speed benchmark for climbing organisms—by 40%, marking it as the fastest and strongest bio-mimetic suction cup-based suction robot to date.

Doxorubicin (Doxo) serves as a standard treatment for colon cancer, yet its clinical efficacy is often limited, prompting interest combination regimens like those incorporating Interleukin-2 (IL-2) to trigger immune activation. This combination is theoretically promising but lacks clear mechanistic understanding. Our research evaluates the combinatorial effects of Doxo and IL-2 within a quantitative mathematical framework, addressing both direct tumor inhibition by Doxo and indirect tumor targeting via IL-2-induced immune stimulation. By applying these dynamics in a single-agent context first, we confirm that doxo effectively reduces tumor burden. Furthermore, single-agent IL-2 induction of robust cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) responses can also suppress tumor growth. Crucially, our combinatorial analysis reveals that concurrent use of both agents significantly delays tumor expansion more effectively than either treatment alone. This enhanced efficacy stems from synergistic anti-tumor activity, a conclusion supported by our data.

Recent studies indicate that minimizing the average Age of Information (AoI) within wireless communication networks requires addressing source coding and channel source decoding independently. Decoding schemes aimed solely at reducing AoI often fail to optimize network throughput efficiently. To resolve this, we introduce a unified framework establishing a specific relationship between AoI and throughput by proposing the concept of Rate-Distortion Efficiency (RDE), where "rate" represents throughput and "distortion" corresponds to the long-term average AoI. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed scheme simultaneously achieves optimal convergence for both minimum AoI and maximum throughput within certain classes. We validate these findings using a packetization model where source data arrives as a Poisson process and decoding events also occur as a random process.

Using a surrogate model trained on outputs from full General Relativity simulations, we forecast the detection capabilities of current and upcoming gravitational-wave interferometers for compact binary systems with masses ranging up to $1000 M_\odot$ and separators extending to $10^{10}\ \text{m}$. Our assessment indicates that, for binaries whose signals reach a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of approximately 8, evolved remnants such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes typically transition from initial eccentricities ($E_i$) of 0.01–0.10 to final eccentricities ($E_f$) of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2}$. Consequently, by the time these binaries become detectable, their orbits are already nearly circular. We further observe that this behavior is largely independent of the specific shape of the detector's noise profile and the binary's mass or coalescence time. These findings support the premise that detectable eccentric binary mergers will be scarce, suggesting that observational efforts should prioritize binaries with significant eccentricities only during the very early stages of their evolution, before detection becomes possible.

We introduce a novel Generative Ensemble framework named DyGED designed for EVent Detection in dynamic graphs. This model addresses limitations in prior methods that often rely on graph neural networks or deep learning; instead, it leverages node and edge generation to transform heterogeneous graphs into scalable substructures. By applying deep learning techniques to this transformation, DyGED isolates key attributes relevant to the original graph while reducing memory requirements. It subsequently locates events within these substructures using a learned model. Empirical results on real-world datasets demonstrate that DyGED surpasses GraphEdge and dy2seq in detection accuracy and operates more efficiently than these baselines and state-of-the-art methods.

A significant hurdle in numerical work regarding radiative hydrodynamic stars is the challenge of accurately capturing both convection and radiation transport mechanisms. Consequently, possessing robust methods for solving complex, nonlinear systems of partial differential equations describing these processes is crucial. This paper introduces a method to validate modern hydrodynamic software through Guderley problem solutions, which model the self-similar implosive shock convergence towards a point. Our findings reveal that self-similar solutions to the radiation-hydrodynamic equations can exhibit oscillatory behaviors in radiation pressure and velocity fields immediately behind the shock, analogous to those observed in ideal magnetohydrodynamics (IMHD). These observations were obtained using LEAP, an advanced radiation-hydrodynamic code developed at the University of Oxford. Additionally, we present new analytical insights into the radiation-governed Guderley problem, including the derivation of an updated, more precise form for the radiation equation of the effective state parameters. We demonstrate that our results align well with previously published literature, thereby reinforcing confidence in numerical implementations within astronomical simulations.

Adenomas are the primary precursors to colorectal cancer; therefore, their precise classification and grading are essential for effective diagnosis and treatment planning. This study introduces an approach utilizing deep neural networks to automatically categorize and assess the grade of adenomas based on endoscopic imagery. The methodology involves first training a deep convolutional neural network on a dataset of endoscopic fundus images to classify images into three categories: normal, adenoma, or cancer. Following this, a deep regression neural network is applied to images classified as adenoma to determine their specific grade. On the dataset employed, this technique achieved an adenoma detection rate (ADR) of 88.5% and a correlation coefficient of 0.82 with a human expert's adenoma grade assessment, corresponding a grade accuracy performance of 75%.

Optimal normalized leakage represents the minimal amount of information disclosed to an attacker regarding a sensitive variable, $S$, resulting from a data processing step, $S \to Y$. In this study, we examine a scenario where an adversary, facing a limited side-information set, $S \to Z$, attempts to decrypt an additional data set, $S \in \mathcal{S}$, after observing $Y$. We investigate the relationship between optimal normalized leakage and optimal compression rates for bounded-length source coding, as well as its connection to optimal conditional extraction. We further extend our analysis to a multi-user setting involving $n$ adversaries, each with distinct side-information, $S \to Z_i$, attempting to recover the source data, $S \in \mathcal{S}$, from the observed output, $Y$. We demonstrate that if every adversary's achievable conditional extraction rate is a vanishingly small fraction of the optimal source compression rate, then the probability distribution within the observed output, $Y$, must be uniform. Additionally, we establish a condition ensuring the validity of the source privacy filter, which dictates the precise distributional requirements of the observed output, $Y$, when only a subset of the adversaries succeeds in their source reconstruction attempts. We introduce a multi-resolution synthetic image generation framework named MrSARP, which utilizes a hierarchical deep-generative model to synthesize images across various scales, from low to high resolution, simultaneously. This approach leverages a hierarchical architecture where a coarse, low-resolution generator feeds into a finer one, allowing MrSARP to manage the multi-resolution task more efficiently than single-resolution methods while also producing realistic high-resolution outcomes. Furthermore, we implement a specific training strategy to enhance the fidelity of the fine-resolution output by isolating and correcting high-frequency details. Our experiments confirm that MrSARP significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in both speed and fidelity in its high-resolution outputs when tasked with multi-resolution image synthesis.

Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms (QAOAs) and other hybrid quantum-classical frameworks face variational optimization challenges that are notoriously difficult for classical optimizers, even on limited quantum hardware. Bayesian optimization mitigates this by leveraging prior parameter estimates to guide the search for superior solutions, yet it demands substantial prior knowledge—particularly for QAOAs which may only access the black-box objective function via measurements. While standard BO approaches demand numerous oracle queries, this paper demonstrates that incorporating Bayesian quadrature enables QAOAs with quadratically fewer parameter oracle calls compared to prior methods, effectively bypassing the need for expensive gradient or finite-difference approximations. Consequently, this research confirms the practical viability of using Bayesian optimization techniques within QAOAs to enhance performance.

This paper presents "PolEllIP," an algorithm designed to find the eight solution points across two elliptic curves defined by general quadratic coefficients. To achieve this, we employ bary elliptic coordinates, mapping each polynomial ellipse equation into the coordinates of five bary elliptic points. By comparing these two sets of coordinates to identify four shared points, we solve for the resulting quartic system using a Wronsk-like determinant. This approach bypasses cumbersome algebraic operations associated with traditional methods, such as implicitizing, substituting quadratically parametrized forms, or computing resultant calculations. We validate the algorithm through tests on various resultants and demonstrate that it correctly yields solutions for intersections of two general quadratics, including all known special scenarios involving conics, circles, ellips, and paraboles.

Reinforcement learning algorithms have become a primary method for addressing the computational challenge of deriving the Gibbs measure's density function, which is derived from the q-function in this context. While these techniques are effective for specific scenarios, they often fail to converge for more complex problems or require extensive experimentation to tune their parameters appropriately. This paper introduces a novel hybrid algorithm that integrates the recursive least squares approach with multiple actor-critic methodologies, specifically incorporating gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, normal equation solution, and Bayesian optimization to enhance both the efficacy and adaptability of reinforcement learning algorithms for optimal policy learning. Through extensive experimentation demonstrated via case studies involving function approximation techniques, our research indicates that the proposed algorithm offers superior computational efficiency compared to existing reinforcement learning algorithms, demonstrating faster convergence rates and improved performance metrics under comparable experimental conditions.

A quantum Monte Carlo method tailored for momentum space that accommodates non-local interactions has been developed and employed to examine the Hubbard model. This approach rationalizes prior findings from the Dynamical Mean-Field Theory of Hubbard Stripes (DMHS) concerning how quantum fluctuations stabilize a stripe-ordered state, explaining the mechanism via a path integral formulation. Furthermore, we propose an alternative computational scheme involving Monte Carlo integration over binary stripe configurations, which samples according to a variational action derived from DMHS. This scheme simulates the stripes effectively in zero spatial dimensions ($d=1$) and one dimension ($d=1$ in context of DMHS usually implies 1D reduction for stripes, but the text says $d=1$ and $d=2$ relative to the parent model dimensions) or more accurately $d=1$ spatial dimensions and $d=2$ spatial dimensions relative to the parent. The DMHS action also serves as a basis for analyzing the thermodynamics of stripe fluctuations via classical Monte Carlo techniques in various dimensions.

This paper introduces a new deep learning framework called label shift adaptation (LSA) specifically designed for identifying and localizing vertebrae across different spinal regions using only sagittal MRI planes generated from single-modality data. By leveraging class activation maps (CAMs) to pinpoint region-relevant features automatically, the model generates refined class-conditional feature maps tailored to specific regions. These maps then inform a novel attention module that aggregates feature diagnostics relevant to the target region, significantly enhancing the accuracy of vertebral identification and localization. When benchmarked against 11 established state-of-the-art techniques using three datasets, our approach achieved average per-case identification and per-centosere accuracy metrics that were 11.5% and 10.5% higher, respectively. We also conducted comprehensive ablation studies to assess the efficacy of our approach's core components alongside comparisons with existing alternatives.

We demonstrate an algebraic and topological framework enabling the computation of asymptotic averages and integrals relevant to correlation analysis within Markovian models. This approach exemplifies a generalised setting adapted from the homological analysis of random walks on finite groups, specifically formulating a homology theory applicable to Markovian models. We establish that, provided a suitable homomorphism exists, this newly defined topological structure aligns perfectly with an associated asymptotic algebra of random variables. Practical implementations are detailed for both finite-state Markov chains and Markovian models constructed on coverings.

We introduce a spatially tailored light-phase profiling technique enabling precise shaping of polariton potential landscapes within all-optical systems. This methodology facilitates the shipping movement of polariton matter waves through complex configurations by tuning the associated lens-like potential through spatial light modulators. The proposed approach is validated using a superfluid Lena image-shaped polariton droplet cluster "cluster," demonstrating scalable control. This high precision control paves the way for shaping and manipulating all-optical quantum networks for applications in quantum sensing, signaling transmission, and other pivotal areas.

The planet K2-22 b, situated in the Kepler field, is hypothesized to be a sub-Neptune with an orbital period of 10.8 days, a period of time that has led to speculation regarding possible mass loss. By utilizing data from the Wide Angle Camera on the W.M. Keck II Telescope, we have gathered high-precision photometry for this target. Our photometric data confirm the existence of transit timing variations (TTVs) and constrain the circumstellar disk around this planet. Specifically, we limit the amount of dust to a relative transit depth of less than 0.0032 (at a 3σ confidence interval), which corresponds to an equivalent planet-to-star mass ratio of $3 \times 10^{-6}$, or roughly 30 times Earth's mass in the disk. Assuming the evaporation rate stems entirely from photoionization, our models suggest the disk dissipates within approximately 100,000 years. Consequently, we conclude that any atmospheric mass loss is negligible, implying that the lifetime of K2-22 b is nearly perpetual.

Although Galileo is celebrated as the father of modern science for his empirical methods, his commitment to establishing fundamental, universal laws was surprisingly inconsistent, despite his extensive use of mathematics to describe nature. His work in the first half of the 17th century sought to counter the Aristotelian view that physical laws varied based on material composition. To achieve this, Galileo attempted to derive the motion laws applicable to all heavy bodies from the study of falling spheres, assuming their behavior was sufficiently similar. His attempt, however, was undermined because his claims about spheres becoming known as such only in the latter half of that century. Consequently, later physicists like Isaac Newton had to begin their analyses with non-similar bodies rather than a uniquely defined category like the "heavy sphere." Newton ultimately succeeded in deriving the laws of motion from "bodies of very small resistance," a classification that more accurately supported the necessary logical premises for universal scientific principles.

Investigating the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) evolution of magnetic islands is vital for understanding energy transport in the solar atmosphere. To address this, a novel numerical model was developed, ranging from macro-scale MHD down to localized kinetic physics at island edges via a 1D fully kinetic solver. This hybrid solver incorporates crucial effects such as magnetic reconnection, particle kinetic instabilities, and anomalous transport. When applied to fully kinetic simulations of magnetic island coalescence—a standard test case examining the interaction between large-scale MHD and microscopic kinetic mechanisms—the model reveals that reducing current width accelerates outer islands toward each other. Upon contact, these islands either merge or split into two smaller islands depending on the specific parameters. Consequently, an initial small island system can evolve into either a single large island or a spectrum of intermediate-sized structures. These findings underscore the significance of coupling macro and micro scales when modeling solar atmospheric transport and highlight the potential utility of fully kinetic simulations of island coalescence for investigating the global emergence and distribution of magnetic islands on the Sun.

Collaborating humans and machines require more than just communication skills; they must also possess the ability to learn from one another how effective partnerships function. This paper introduces a specific learning framework designed for digital assistants to acquire effective collaboration strategies over time. By explicitly model the communication process between a agent and its human partner through a Markov model, we can identify interaction patterns that correlate with successful outcomes. These effective communication dynamics are subsequently distilled into simplified representations of task progress—such as step-wise progress models—that the assistant can utilize for making quick, resource-efficient decisions during tasks. By deploying this learned logic, we enable the assistant to acquire collaboration skills, build intuitive understanding, and even forecast human actions without imposing additional communication overhead.
